title: Pathology Fellowship
level: Consolidated institutional fellowship-directory category (eight distinct clinical physician fellowship offerings; not one clinical specialty)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Medical degree or equivalent and prior pathology foundations assumed; this is not an eligibility rule for any fellowship.
Basic cell biology, anatomy, histology, immunology, microbiology and laboratory statistics.
Introductory familiarity with diagnostic reasoning and professional confidentiality.
objectives: Use a structured specimen-to-report reasoning sequence and state limitations.
Integrate morphology with context and targeted ancillary testing across listed fields.
Use current ABPath blueprints to organize study without claiming exam readiness.
Distinguish the institution’s exact fellowship offering, ACGME accreditation, and board examinations.
Interpret clinical laboratory and quality-system questions at a conceptual level.
Use authentic cases only through lawful links and case-specific permission.

units.title: Diagnostic method, specimen lifecycle and report quality
objectives: Trace specimen identification, fixation, grossing, processing, slide creation and result communication.
Distinguish preanalytic, analytic and postanalytic error and specify a safe escalation.
Construct a concise, uncertainty-calibrated pathology report.
topics: Specimen adequacy, chain of identity, fixation, sampling, tissue stewardship, turnaround time, report components, amended reports, consultation, quality assurance.
casePractice: Fictional specimen-identity and adequacy vignettes; no real records.
units.assessment: Submit a one-page workflow map and structured report from a fictional low-information specimen. Rubric (20): identity/adequacy 5; diagnostic uncertainty 5; clinically useful structured result 5; escalation and QA 5.

units.title: General pathology, injury and repair
objectives: Explain reversible and irreversible cellular injury, inflammation, repair and adaptation.
Use morphology and clinical context to discriminate common injury patterns.
topics: Cell stress, necrosis/apoptosis, acute/chronic inflammation, wound repair, hemodynamic disorders, immune injury, infection and inherited disease.
casePractice: Fictional morphology-descriptor exercise using legally open teaching slides only.
units.assessment: Compare three fictional injury patterns with mechanism, differential and limitation. Rubric: mechanism 6; differential 6; morphology/context 4; uncertainty 4.

units.title: Surgical pathology, gross-to-micro correlation
objectives: Build a differential diagnosis from a pattern and site rather than a single stain.
Select a focused, hypothesis-driven ancillary panel and interpret results in context.
topics: Sampling/gross description, epithelial and mesenchymal patterns, benign/malignant distinctions, margins, grade/stage boundaries, immunohistochemistry, molecular correlation.
casePractice: PathPresenter Public cases; use links; check case-specific de-identification and terms.
units.assessment: Defend an original fictional differential and stain plan. Rubric: pattern recognition 5; differential 5; test selection 5; appropriate reporting limits 5.

units.title: Cytopathology and aspiration specimens
objectives: Apply adequacy and specimen triage principles to exfoliative and aspirate cytology.
Use reporting-system categories with appropriate risk language and clinical correlation.
topics: FNA, liquid-based cytology, cell blocks, adequacy, thyroid/salivary/pancreatic cytology, gynecologic screening concepts, ancillary tests, sampling limitations.
casePractice: PathPresenter Public; CAP cases member-restricted. Never copy images.
units.assessment: Categorize 4 fictional cytology scenarios and propose next-step communication. Rubric: adequacy 5; classification 5; differential 5; limitation/safety 5.

units.title: Breast and gastrointestinal pathology (selective focus)
objectives: Recognize common breast and GI diagnostic patterns and reporting implications.
Separate institutional fellowship training from separately board-certified subspecialty status.
topics: Breast lesions and radiology-pathology correlation; GI mucosal biopsies, polyps, inflammatory patterns, pancreatic lesions; specimen/report essentials.
casePractice: Linked free pathCast cases/lectures; CAP library not freely open.
units.assessment: Write paired short differential matrices (breast and GI) from fictional descriptions. Rubric: differential breadth 6; relevant ancillary/clinical correlation 5; report language 5; uncertainty 4.

units.title: Hematopathology and blood disorders
objectives: Integrate morphology, flow cytometry, immunophenotype, cytogenetics and molecular results without treating one test as definitive.
Distinguish marrow/lymph-node patterns and identify urgent communication needs.
topics: Hematopoiesis, reactive vs neoplastic, lymphoma/leukemia classification, marrow sampling, flow, molecular correlation, current WHO/ICC distinction, transfusion overlap.
casePractice: PathPresenter Public lymph node/marrow cases; verify individual licenses.
units.assessment: Create a fictional integrated diagnostic work-up with a one-paragraph report. Rubric: morphology 4; integration 6; classification qualifier 5; limitations/communication 5.

units.title: Transfusion medicine and blood bank
objectives: Apply compatibility logic, component-selection principles and reaction workup sequence.
Prioritize immediate safety and laboratory communication in suspected transfusion reactions.
topics: ABO/Rh, antibody screen/identification, crossmatch concepts, component indications, hemolytic reactions, inventory/quality, apheresis overview, transfusion regulations.
casePractice: Fictional reaction scenarios; no patient chart details or treatment orders.
units.assessment: Solve 3 fictional pretransfusion/reaction scenarios. Rubric: compatibility logic 6; differential/workup 6; communication 4; appropriate non-prescriptive boundary 4.

units.title: Clinical microbiology and medical microbiology fellowship concepts
objectives: Use specimen/site, host and test properties to interpret microbiology results.
Explain susceptibility-testing limits and stewardship communication.
topics: Specimen quality, Gram stain/culture, blood cultures, bacteriology, mycology, virology, parasitology, susceptibility testing, molecular diagnostics, contamination vs infection.
casePractice: CDC DPDx linked teaching resources; no reproduced clinical records.
units.assessment: Interpret fictional culture/molecular-result combinations. Rubric: specimen context 5; test interpretation 5; differential 5; limits/communication 5.

units.title: Dermatopathology
objectives: Approach inflammatory dermatoses by reaction pattern and clinicopathologic correlation.
Construct a neoplasm differential while avoiding overconfident classification from incomplete findings.
topics: Interface, spongiotic, psoriasiform, lichenoid, vasculopathic patterns; melanocytic lesions and tumors; biopsy site/level and ancillary tests.
casePractice: PathPresenter Public skin cases; verify de-identification and individual reuse terms.
units.assessment: Create a reaction-pattern differential from fictional microscopic descriptors. Rubric: pattern 6; differential 6; ancillary correlation 4; qualifier 4.

units.title: Neuropathology
objectives: Localize key CNS specimen contexts and distinguish tumor, vascular, inflammatory and degenerative diagnostic questions.
Integrate morphology with molecular classification without exceeding evidence.
topics: CNS tumors, glial/embryonal/meningeal lesions, infection, vascular injury, neurodegeneration, intraoperative consultation, molecular testing.
casePractice: PathPresenter Public CNS cases; link only, verify public status and reuse limits.
units.assessment: Compare fictional CNS differential diagnoses and state what additional data is needed. Rubric: localization 4; pattern 5; molecular integration 5; limitations 6.

units.title: Quality, laboratory management, informatics and molecular diagnostics
objectives: Apply quality systems to a laboratory event and describe a corrective-action cycle.
Assess molecular-test validity and reporting boundaries.
topics: Quality indicators, proficiency testing, accreditation/regulation, safety, informatics, LIS, data integrity, validation, variant nomenclature principles, test limitations and governance.
casePractice: Fictional QA scenarios only; no protected records.
units.assessment: Write a root-cause analysis and minimal validation plan for a hypothetical assay. Rubric: problem framing 4; evidence/measure 5; corrective action 5; validation/communication 6.

units.title: Integrated unknowns, consultation and professional limits
objectives: Synthesize morphology, clinical history, laboratory data and uncertainty in a defensible differential.
Explain the distinctions among a clinical fellowship, ACGME accreditation and ABPath certification.
topics: Integrated AP/CP unknowns; consultation; conflicting results; age/context; communication; board blueprint use; ethics, image licensing, scope of self-study.
boardDomains: ABPath primary and relevant subspecialty blueprints
casePractice: Fictional composite cases; no patient images unless lawfully linked and case terms permit viewing.
units.assessment: Final portfolio: three fictional consult cases, evidence matrix and reflective limitation note. Rubric: diagnostic reasoning 8; evidence integration 4; report quality 4; boundaries/licensing/uncertainty 4.

assignment.title: Integrated fictional consultation portfolio
deliverables: Three fictional cases: one morphologic, one clinical laboratory/transfusion/microbiology, and one ancillary-test discordance.
For each: problem representation, adequacy/limitations, differential, focused tests, concise report and communication/escalation note.
A short audit of one ABPath blueprint and one institutional fellowship offering, with exact boundary between public evidence and unresolved details.
assignment.rubric: 100 points: reasoning and differential 25; integration of test/context 20; report clarity and limitation calibration 20; quality/safety communication 15; appropriate sources and current qualifiers 10; distinction among directory/accreditation/board status 10. This is a self-study rubric, not a validated competency or entrustment assessment.

assessment.format: Unit quizzes and final portfolio; all questions original and educational.
assessment.passingRule: No pass threshold has been validated; formative self-check only.
assessment.limits: Not official board questions, not a predictor of board performance, not clinical credentialing.

studyHours.status: Study plan, not observed clinical or contact hours
studyHours.allocation: 12 units × 10 hours: approximately 2 hours linked lectures/reading, 4 hours case/problem work, 2 hours assessment/feedback, and 2 hours review/portfolio. Actual study time will vary. Video hours are separately reported.

unitMap.text: Diagnostic method, specimen lifecycle and report quality
coveredTopics: Specimen adequacy, chain of identity, fixation, sampling, tissue stewardship, turnaround time, report components, amended reports, consultation, quality assurance.

unitMap.text: General pathology, injury and repair
coveredTopics: Cell stress, necrosis/apoptosis, acute/chronic inflammation, wound repair, hemodynamic disorders, immune injury, infection and inherited disease.

unitMap.text: Surgical pathology, gross-to-micro correlation
coveredTopics: Sampling/gross description, epithelial and mesenchymal patterns, benign/malignant distinctions, margins, grade/stage boundaries, immunohistochemistry, molecular correlation.

unitMap.text: Cytopathology and aspiration specimens
coveredTopics: FNA, liquid-based cytology, cell blocks, adequacy, thyroid/salivary/pancreatic cytology, gynecologic screening concepts, ancillary tests, sampling limitations.

unitMap.text: Breast and gastrointestinal pathology (selective focus)
coveredTopics: Breast lesions and radiology-pathology correlation; GI mucosal biopsies, polyps, inflammatory patterns, pancreatic lesions; specimen/report essentials.

unitMap.text: Hematopathology and blood disorders
coveredTopics: Hematopoiesis, reactive vs neoplastic, lymphoma/leukemia classification, marrow sampling, flow, molecular correlation, current WHO/ICC distinction, transfusion overlap.

unitMap.text: Transfusion medicine and blood bank
coveredTopics: ABO/Rh, antibody screen/identification, crossmatch concepts, component indications, hemolytic reactions, inventory/quality, apheresis overview, transfusion regulations.

unitMap.text: Clinical microbiology and medical microbiology fellowship concepts
coveredTopics: Specimen quality, Gram stain/culture, blood cultures, bacteriology, mycology, virology, parasitology, susceptibility testing, molecular diagnostics, contamination vs infection.

unitMap.text: Dermatopathology
coveredTopics: Interface, spongiotic, psoriasiform, lichenoid, vasculopathic patterns; melanocytic lesions and tumors; biopsy site/level and ancillary tests.

unitMap.text: Neuropathology
coveredTopics: CNS tumors, glial/embryonal/meningeal lesions, infection, vascular injury, neurodegeneration, intraoperative consultation, molecular testing.

unitMap.text: Quality, laboratory management, informatics and molecular diagnostics
coveredTopics: Quality indicators, proficiency testing, accreditation/regulation, safety, informatics, LIS, data integrity, validation, variant nomenclature principles, test limitations and governance.

unitMap.text: Integrated unknowns, consultation and professional limits
coveredTopics: Integrated AP/CP unknowns; consultation; conflicting results; age/context; communication; board blueprint use; ethics, image licensing, scope of self-study.

topicGaps: 21.73 verified free external specialty-video hours are available, all mapped to hematopathology (unit 6); the 36-hour target therefore retains an actual 14.27-hour residual. No planned/original script minutes count toward ready video hours.

Recordings do not supply balanced hour coverage across diagnostic workflow, general pathology, surgical pathology, cytopathology, selective breast/GI, transfusion medicine, microbiology, dermatopathology, neuropathology, quality/informatics and integrated consult domains. Those topic gaps remain despite the hematopathology expansion.
PathCast and other named open archives have relevant topics but item-level unique ID/runtime evidence was incomplete; do not count those entries until direct URLs and public duration can be checked.

Programme-specific rotations, offering-level accreditation, training duration and eligibility details are not disclosed by the category-level BIDMC page; verify with institution and board. No eligibility or accreditation inference is made.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

practiceQuestions.stem: A gross room receives two unlabeled containers from the same procedure. What is the safest immediate laboratory action?

options.text: Accession both under the likely patient based on the requisition.
Ask a colleague to infer which tissue matches each label.
Hold processing, isolate the specimens, and resolve identity with the submitting team under local policy.
Discard both specimens without notification.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Specimen identity is a prerequisite to diagnosis. Stop and resolve discrepancy through documented local escalation; never infer identity.

practiceQuestions.stem: A biopsy has extensive crush artifact and scant viable tissue. Which report approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Provide an unqualified definitive tumor subtype.
Describe adequacy/artifact, state the limits of interpretation, and recommend correlation or additional material as appropriate.
Order every available stain without a hypothesis.
Ignore the artifact because immunostains can always resolve it.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A report should state material limitations and avoid unsupported certainty; further testing or sampling is contextual, not automatic.

practiceQuestions.stem: An aspirate is sparsely cellular. Which first question should guide interpretation?

options.text: Which molecular panel has the most genes?
Is the specimen adequate and representative for the clinical question?
Can a malignancy be ruled out from the lack of atypia?
Can the reporting category be selected from imaging alone?

practiceQuestions.rationale: Adequacy and representativeness are central in cytology. A scant sample cannot automatically exclude disease.

practiceQuestions.stem: A lymph node shows atypical lymphoid cells; flow cytometry is noncontributory. What is the best reasoning?

options.text: Flow excludes lymphoma.
Integrate morphology, immunophenotype, clinical context, and any indicated cytogenetic/molecular studies; qualify unresolved uncertainty.
Assign a subtype using one marker.
Repeat the same test until it is positive.

practiceQuestions.rationale: No single ancillary test overrides discordant morphology/context; integrated classification and explicit uncertainty are appropriate.

practiceQuestions.stem: A post-transfusion patient develops fever and hypotension. Which laboratory response is most appropriate?

options.text: Assume a febrile nonhemolytic reaction and close the case.
Promptly notify the responsible clinical team and transfusion service, stop/secure the implicated component per local protocol, and initiate the defined reaction workup.
Issue another unit from the same donor without review.
Rely on a retrospective antibody screen only.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Possible acute reaction requires immediate clinical and transfusion-service communication and a protocol-based investigation; this educational item is not a treatment directive.

practiceQuestions.stem: A positive blood culture grows a common skin organism in only one bottle. What most improves interpretation?

options.text: Organism name alone.
Specimen collection quality, number/time of positive sets, host/context, and concordant findings.
Assume contamination in every case.
Treat every positive bottle as bloodstream infection.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Culture interpretation integrates pretest context, number of sets, collection and clinical information; no single heuristic is universally decisive.

practiceQuestions.stem: A skin biopsy shows a lichenoid/interface pattern. What is the most defensible next interpretive step?

options.text: Name a specific disorder from this pattern alone.
Use pattern to form a differential and correlate with distribution, clinical details, and targeted ancillary findings.
Use a stain panel without stating a differential.
Ignore site and clinical history.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Reaction patterns organize but do not uniquely determine the diagnosis; clinicopathologic correlation narrows the differential.

practiceQuestions.stem: A brain tumor has a characteristic morphology, but molecular data conflict with the favored entity. How should this be handled?

options.text: Morphology always overrides molecular results.
Molecular results always override morphology.
Check specimen identity/assay quality and classification criteria, integrate all findings, and state uncertainty or defer classification if unresolved.
Choose the more familiar label.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Modern integrated classification requires valid, concordant evidence; discordance triggers review and qualified reporting rather than forced certainty.

practiceQuestions.stem: An assay is introduced after a major reagent/platform change. Which evidence is most pertinent before clinical reporting?

options.text: A single normal control run.
Documented validation/verification appropriate to intended use, with performance characteristics and quality controls.
Vendor brochure alone.
Retrospective reassurance after first reports.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Changes affecting test performance require documented verification/validation appropriate to the test and jurisdiction before clinical use.

practiceQuestions.stem: A pathology fellowship category lists GI and breast training. What may a learner infer about board credentialing?

options.text: Each listing guarantees a separate board examination.
A named institutional fellowship and a board subspecialty are different; verify the current certifying-board list for the exact field.
ACGME listing alone grants board eligibility to every applicant.
Completion of this independent course establishes eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Institutional offerings, ACGME accreditation and board certificates are distinct. ABPath subspecialty exam list does not include breast/GI pathology as separate named exams.

topicGaps: Public recordings are not a complete residency curriculum and do not offer observed microscope sign-out, gross-room practice, autopsy supervision, clinical-laboratory call, or observed competency assessment.
Counts of public talks and runtimes do not prove current classification coverage or a defined educational sequence; some recordings may use older terminology. Check current primary sources.

The ABPath AP/CP descriptions cover much more than any finite video set; accessible public teaching videos may underrepresent forensic/autopsy, analytical validation, laboratory regulations, body-fluid microscopy, cytogenetics, safety and informatics.
No individual lecture is a substitute for local SOPs, accession systems, current CAP/CLIA requirements, institution-specific protocols, or supervised clinical communication.
Public educational cases may use original institutional material; licensing and patient de-identification claims remain with the source host. This course does not republish slides, images or records.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Scope is the Johns Hopkins clinical physician pathology residency and its AP, CP, AP/CP, AP/NP training variants. The source packet’s Johns Hopkins clinical residency page confirms ACGME-accredited status and four years for the directory listing. The pathology department curriculum has more granular track names and blocks. The institution also lists named postdoctoral fellowships (for example breast, GI/liver, GU, renal, gynecologic, surgical, hematopathology, cytopathology, forensic, neuropathology, medical microbiology, molecular genetic pathology, transfusion medicine and clinical chemistry); these are fellowships/extension tracks, not silently recast as residency specialties, nor all assumed to have separate ABPath exams. Individual PhD/DVM/research fellowships are research/non-physician supplements rather than physician residency credentials. “Pathology” directory label is not itself a distinct board certificate. Board examinations and published ACGME program categories differ from Hopkins local track names.

Full playback of every entry was not retested individually; free access status means public YouTube playlist listing and no course enrollment, not a guarantee against later removal, age/region restrictions or changes.
The public Hopkins curriculum describes local rotations and blocks, not total teaching hours or an exhaustive lecture inventory.

practiceQuestions.stem: A platelet transfusion is underway when the recipient develops fever and rigors. Bacterial contamination is among the plausible explanations. Which immediate response best matches current CDC guidance?

options.text: Continue slowly while waiting for a post-transfusion culture.
Stop the transfusion, save the component for investigation, and obtain recipient blood cultures; retain isolates and follow local escalation protocols.
Discard the remaining component and collect only a new CBC.
Assume a febrile nonhemolytic reaction and resume after symptoms settle.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC recommends immediately stopping transfusions when bacterial contamination is suspected, saving the component, obtaining recipient blood cultures, and preserving isolates for investigation. Clinical response and local reaction protocol remain clinician-led.

practiceQuestions.stem: ABPath describes its AP examination as including written/practical and virtual-microscopy sections. Which statement is accurate for the AP/CP pathway?

options.text: One combined examination replaces both AP and CP examinations.
The AP and CP are distinct examinations; ABPath issues the combined AP/CP certificate only after both examinations are passed and requirements are met.
AP/CP certification is available without an MD/DO or medical license.
The CP examination is replaced by the subspecialty hematopathology examination.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPath describes distinct AP and CP exam formats and states combined AP/CP certification follows passage of both examinations. Eligibility also requires qualifying medical education, licensure, and training.

practiceQuestions.stem: A nonwaived chemistry analyzer produces a sudden shift in control results after maintenance. What is the best laboratory-quality response?

options.text: Release patient results because the calibrator passed last month.
Apply the laboratory’s validated QC and troubleshooting SOP, assess whether the affected run is valid, document the investigation, and release only when requirements are met.
Replace all patient reference intervals.
Use a verbal assurance from the vendor and omit documentation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CLIA requires QC procedures that monitor accuracy and precision of the complete testing process. This fictional workflow question does not prescribe a single local QC frequency; use current local SOPs and regulatory requirements.

practiceQuestions.stem: A tissue specimen arrives with a label that conflicts with the requisition. Which first step is safest?

options.text: Choose the likely label based on histology and proceed.
Stop processing under the affected workflow, preserve the specimen, and resolve identity through the institution’s documented chain-of-custody and escalation procedure.
Correct the label from memory after asking a colleague.
Issue a provisional malignant diagnosis to prompt attention.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The identity discrepancy is a preanalytic safety issue; do not infer or silently amend patient identity. Follow the institution’s validated identification and escalation SOP. This is an original systems-safety item, not a quoted board question.

practiceQuestions.stem: A small core biopsy shows a high-grade malignant neoplasm, but the sample is scant and morphology alone cannot reliably distinguish two plausible lineages. What is the best next diagnostic approach?

options.text: Order a broad panel without considering tissue depletion.
Review adequacy and clinical context, prioritize a focused differential-driven ancillary strategy with the team, and state the limitations if unresolved.
Call the tumor type definitively based solely on the most common diagnosis at that site.
Use a treatment regimen as a diagnostic test.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AP exam competencies encompass diagnosis across specimen types and ancillary studies. A defensible approach preserves limited tissue, answers a defined question, and communicates uncertainty rather than asserting a lineage unsupported by the specimen.

practiceQuestions.stem: A clinician asks whether a finding in a molecular report proves a germline predisposition. The assay was performed on tumor-only material and no paired normal sample is available. What is the most accurate response?

options.text: Yes; every pathogenic tumor variant is inherited.
No; tumor-only testing cannot by itself establish germline status, and the assay/report limitations and appropriate follow-up should be communicated.
Yes, if the variant allele fraction is exactly 50%.
No, because molecular results have no diagnostic use.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Tumor-only sequencing does not by itself establish whether a detected variant is somatic or germline. Interpretation depends on assay design, data, and follow-up; do not use allele fraction alone as proof.

practiceQuestions.stem: A laboratory must interpret an elevated test result near a decision threshold. Which additional principle is most important before treating the value as biologically definitive?

options.text: Assume all assay methods and specimen conditions are interchangeable.
Review analytical performance, preanalytic conditions, interferences, method-specific limitations, and clinical context.
Ignore controls if the result is clinically plausible.
Convert the numeric result into a disease diagnosis without a differential.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The CP domains include analytical methods, specimen collection, statistics, and diagnostic interpretation of laboratory data. A result must be interpreted in context of method and quality.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes what a public free pathology image repository permits by default?

options.text: Any free-to-view image may be copied into a new course.
Linking/viewing does not automatically authorize reuse; follow the repository’s explicit license and keep images on the source site unless reuse permission is clear.
An image becomes public domain as soon as it is used in education.
De-identification eliminates copyright restrictions.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free access is not a license to copy. PathologyOutlines explicitly protects content, permits linking with stated attribution/no-charge conditions, and applies specific image-use limits. Patient privacy and copyright are separate requirements.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the ABPath CP primary exam content categories on the official exam-description page?

options.text: Microbiology and hematopathology are omitted.
Blood banking/transfusion, chemistry and immunopathology/serology, hematopathology, medical microbiology, and laboratory management are included.
The CP exam tests only transfusion medicine.
The content is restricted to image interpretation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPath describes CP content across those five named areas and includes problem-solving material such as images, graphs, charts and laboratory data. The source provides approximate weightings, not a guarantee about any individual examination.

practiceQuestions.stem: An educational self-assessment learner has not completed supervised rotations, case logs, medical school or licensure. What can this course legitimately claim?

options.text: The learner is now eligible to sit for an ABPath exam.
The learner has demonstrated procedural competence.
The learner may use the materials for independent education; it cannot establish accredited training, licensure, board eligibility, or clinical competence.
Completion guarantees passing every pathology board.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPath eligibility requires qualifying medical education, licensure and accredited training (and primary-certification-specific requirements); an independent course cannot substitute for these. The course is not accredited GME or a competence credential.

topicGaps: Added distinct free recordings improve coverage of kidney biopsy IF/EM, broad nephritic and tubulointerstitial patterns, lupus histopathology and acute allograft T-cell-mediated rejection. Each mapping is adjunctive and does not replace current classification or disease-specific guidance.

Unresolved recorded-topic gaps include focused current IgAN/IgAV and Oxford scoring; ANCA/anti-GBM pathology; MCD/FSGS/membranous interpretation beyond existing general recordings; monoclonal and organized-deposit typing; diabetic, hereditary and vascular disease; transplant AMR/Banff update, infection and ancillary/molecular testing; specimen triage, QC, autopsy/excision, and integrated reporting.

Verified public recording total is still below 36 hours. The exact observed-ledger deficit remains a real gap; the planned original clips are unrendered production targets and do not close it. Do not count repeated playlist items, trailers, access-restricted media, the authored scripts, or linked readings as viewing time.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 42-year-old with nephrotic-range proteinuria has segmental sclerosis in one glomerulus. Which interpretation is safest?

options.text: This morphology proves primary FSGS.
FSGS is a lesion requiring clinical, IF/EM, sampling, and secondary/genetic context.
The biopsy excludes a podocytopathy.
It establishes membranous nephropathy.

practiceQuestions.rationale: FSGS is a histologic lesion/pattern; etiology requires integrated evidence and focal disease may be undersampled.

practiceQuestions.stem: A native biopsy shows linear IgG along GBM with necrotizing crescents. Which category is most directly supported?

options.text: Anti-GBM disease pattern; correlate with serology and context.
IgA nephropathy.
Membranous nephropathy by default.
Pauci-immune GN.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Linear GBM IgG with necrotizing/crescentic GN raises anti-GBM disease; differential and serology still matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: A kidney biopsy has granular IgA-dominant mesangial staining. What is the best next reasoning step?

options.text: Call IgA nephropathy without further context.
Integrate LM/EM, clinical setting, and exclude mimics such as infection-related GN.
Call lupus nephritis automatically.
Infer systemic IgA vasculitis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: IgA-dominant IF is not uniquely diagnostic. Correlate morphology, deposit location and clinical setting.

practiceQuestions.stem: What does a negative IF result by itself establish?

options.text: It excludes immune-mediated disease.
It may support a pauci-immune pattern if technically adequate, but needs LM/EM and context.
It proves minimal-change disease.
It proves anti-GBM disease.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Negative/limited IF must be interpreted with specimen adequacy and other modalities; it is not disease proof.

practiceQuestions.stem: In an allograft biopsy, a Banff lesion score is observed. How should it be used?

options.text: As a diagnosis without context.
Apply current Banff definitions and integrate other morphologic, serologic, and ancillary evidence.
Use the 2018 guide only; it supersedes future updates.
Ignore recurrent/de novo GN.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Banff lesion scores contribute to diagnostic categories but are not sufficient by themselves; consult current guide.

practiceQuestions.stem: A specimen has only scant glomeruli and no EM tissue. What is the appropriate reporting habit?

options.text: Declare no disease.
State adequacy and modality limitations and qualify the differential.
Infer EM findings from LM.
Count a planned scan as evidence.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Renal lesions can be focal. Explicitly report tissue and modality limits rather than infer unobserved findings.

practiceQuestions.stem: A biopsy shows full-house-like IF. Which statement is correct?

options.text: This is independently pathognomonic for lupus.
It is a pattern that can support lupus in context but is not independently definitive.
It excludes infection.
It proves class IV lupus nephritis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Full-house staining is supportive but requires clinicopathologic correlation and broader differential.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which approach best distinguishes deposit diseases?

options.text: Use LM alone.
Integrate LM distribution, IF composition/restriction, EM location/organization and clinical data.
Use light-chain ratio only.
Assume all organized deposits are amyloid.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Integrated morphology, IF, ultrastructure, and clinical context classify deposits; ancillary typing may be needed.

title: Transfusion Medicine Fellowship
prerequisites: Graduate-level medical/pathology or hematology knowledge; foundational physiology, hematology, immunology, laboratory medicine and clinical reasoning.
Recommended academic level: post-MD/DO or senior pathology/hematology trainee; this is self-study, not a clinical placement.
Do not interpret course completion as fellowship eligibility, patient-care authorization, laboratory sign-out authority or procedural competence.
objectives: Explain donor-to-recipient systems, component production, storage, labeling, inventory, quality and regulatory interfaces.
Reason through ABO/Rh discrepancy and red-cell alloantibody problems using safe, explicit evidence steps.
Select an educational next-step framework for compatibility testing, suspected reactions and hemovigilance classification.
Compare component-transfusion evidence and patient blood management with population and patient-specific limits.
Describe donor operations, transfusion-transmitted infection control, therapeutic apheresis and cellular-therapy interfaces.
Interpret board-domain knowledge without claiming that self-study substitutes for accredited, supervised training.

units.title: Transfusion service systems, quality and consultation
objectives: Map the hospital transfusion service lifecycle and interfaces with clinical teams.
Frame a concise, evidence-seeking transfusion consultation and document uncertainty.
topics: Laboratory and clinical interfaces; ordering and specimen identity; inventory and stewardship; emergency release; quality indicators; transfusion committee; incident learning.
units.casePractice: Transfusion-service workflow map plus a written consult response to a constructed scenario.
units.assessment: Workflow completeness, safety escalation, source currency and clear limits.
prerequisites: Graduate-level medicine/pathology or hematology; foundational hematology, physiology, immunology, and laboratory medicine. This independent study sequence does not establish clinical eligibility.

units.title: Blood components, preparation, storage and selection
objectives: Compare component content, modifications, storage and expected clinical purpose.
Select a component for a vignette while stating indication-specific uncertainty.
topics: RBCs, platelets, plasma, cryoprecipitate, whole blood; leukoreduction, irradiation, washing, volume reduction, pathogen reduction; storage and transport; labeling and traceability.
units.casePractice: Component selection matrix and short justification for five fictional orders.
units.assessment: Accurate attributes, correct source linkage, appropriate contraindication cautions.
prerequisites: Graduate-level medicine/pathology or hematology; foundational hematology, physiology, immunology, and laboratory medicine. This independent study sequence does not establish clinical eligibility.

units.title: ABO/Rh immunohematology and genetics
objectives: Interpret ABO discrepancies and RhD variants using a structured differential.
Explain antigen/antibody compatibility and genotype-informed selection limits.
topics: ABO genetics/forward-reverse typing; Rh and weak D; clinically significant antigens; dosage, phase, enzyme effects; phenotype/genotype; rare phenotypes.
units.casePractice: Annotated fictional ABO discrepancy and Rh variant reasoning worksheet.
units.assessment: Stepwise reasoning, no unsupported universal rule, source and date checks.
prerequisites: Graduate-level medicine/pathology or hematology; foundational hematology, physiology, immunology, and laboratory medicine. This independent study sequence does not establish clinical eligibility.

units.title: Pretransfusion testing and complex antibody identification
objectives: Choose a safe sequence for type-and-screen, antibody investigation and compatibility testing.
Resolve a panel using rule-outs, dosage, autocontrol/DAT and clinical history.
topics: Specimen identification/validity; antibody screen; panel interpretation; transfusion history; adsorption/elution; warm autoantibodies; cold interference; electronic/immediate-spin/serologic crossmatch; emergency release.
units.casePractice: Complete a linked, fictional antibody-panel exercise; explain each exclusion and issue.
units.assessment: Panel logic and safe product recommendation; candidate is not assessed on leaked board items.
prerequisites: Graduate-level medicine/pathology or hematology; foundational hematology, physiology, immunology, and laboratory medicine. This independent study sequence does not establish clinical eligibility.

units.title: RBC alloimmunization, delayed reactions and HDFN
objectives: Distinguish anamnestic alloimmunization from acute immune hemolysis using timeline and tests.
Describe maternal antibody screening and fetal/newborn risk assessment at a high level.
topics: Alloantibody evanescence; delayed hemolytic/serologic reaction; DAT/elution; antigen-negative selection; anti-D prophylaxis principles; HDFN evaluation and transfusion-support concepts.
units.casePractice: Fictional timeline with serial serology and a safe next-test/consult plan.
units.assessment: Separates evidence from inference, preserves obstetric/neonatal specialist oversight.
prerequisites: Graduate-level medicine/pathology or hematology; foundational hematology, physiology, immunology, and laboratory medicine. This independent study sequence does not establish clinical eligibility.

units.title: Component therapy, thresholds and patient blood management
objectives: Evaluate RBC/platelet/plasma/fibrinogen use against evidence, clinical context and alternatives.
Explain a restrictive strategy without converting a population threshold into an automatic order.
topics: RBC evidence and 2023 guideline context; platelet transfusion; plasma/coagulation; cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen; anemia and blood conservation; perioperative/ICU context; informed decision-making.
units.casePractice: Critique a fictional multi-order audit sample, using rationale and uncertainty.
units.assessment: Uses evidence/current guideline context; distinguishes recommendation from bedside decision.
prerequisites: Graduate-level medicine/pathology or hematology; foundational hematology, physiology, immunology, and laboratory medicine. This independent study sequence does not establish clinical eligibility.

units.title: Acute and delayed transfusion reactions; hemovigilance
objectives: Build a differential and first-response investigation for a suspected reaction.
Apply CDC NHSN v3.0 categories, timing and reporting cautions without conflating surveillance with diagnosis.
topics: AHTR, FNHTR, allergic/anaphylactic, TACO, TRALI, TAD, septic reaction, delayed hemolytic/serologic, TA-GVHD, PTP; stop/notify/verify/investigate as local policy; severity/imputability.
units.casePractice: Classify four fictional reactions using the current CDC protocol and defend the differential.
units.assessment: Correct time windows/criteria, high-risk escalation, surveillance vs diagnosis distinction.
prerequisites: Graduate-level medicine/pathology or hematology; foundational hematology, physiology, immunology, and laboratory medicine. This independent study sequence does not establish clinical eligibility.

units.title: Transfusion-transmitted infection, donor safety and product safety
objectives: Trace a suspected transfusion-transmitted infection across recipient, component and donor investigation.
Use current FDA donor guidance and distinguish guidance from binding regulations.
topics: Donor eligibility; testing; infectious risk mitigation; bacterial contamination of platelets; lookback/traceback; reporting; emerging pathogens; FDA guidance currency.
units.casePractice: Draft a fictional lookback decision tree and data-minimization checklist.
units.assessment: Traceability and regulator-source accuracy; no real patient/donor identifiers.
prerequisites: Graduate-level medicine/pathology or hematology; foundational hematology, physiology, immunology, and laboratory medicine. This independent study sequence does not establish clinical eligibility.

units.title: Donor operations, collection and blood center interface
objectives: Explain collection pathways, component preparation and donor operations at a systems level.
Identify how donor safety and product quality shape inventory and practice.
topics: Whole-blood/apheresis donation; eligibility; collection; processing; storage/distribution; donor reactions; blood center-hospital interface; supply constraints and contingency planning.
units.casePractice: Process map linking donor collection to issue/traceback; identify two failure controls.
units.assessment: Process accuracy, safety controls, avoidance of institution-specific assumptions.
prerequisites: Graduate-level medicine/pathology or hematology; foundational hematology, physiology, immunology, and laboratory medicine. This independent study sequence does not establish clinical eligibility.

units.title: Therapeutic apheresis and clinical consultation
objectives: Relate indication, procedure, modality and expected effect for common therapeutic apheresis consultations.
Recognize citrate, vascular access, hemodynamic and procedure-related risk domains.
topics: Therapeutic plasma exchange; RBC exchange; leukapheresis; photopheresis; collection vs therapeutic procedures; consultation and coordination; monitoring and adverse events.
units.casePractice: Compare three fictional consultation requests and identify needed clinical facts before recommendation.
units.assessment: Indication reasoning, procedural restraint, consultation boundaries, source-backed claims.
prerequisites: Graduate-level medicine/pathology or hematology; foundational hematology, physiology, immunology, and laboratory medicine. This independent study sequence does not establish clinical eligibility.

units.title: Hematopoietic transplantation, immunogenetics and cell therapy
objectives: Explain key transfusion-support principles around HSCT and cellular therapies.
Describe HLA/immunogenetics interfaces and product-chain quality concepts.
topics: HLA matching and antibody context; HSCT support; ABO mismatch; cellular products; collection, processing, cryopreservation, release/labeling, chain of identity/custody; gene-modified therapies.
units.casePractice: Construct a fictional product chain-of-identity checklist and transplant-support questions.
units.assessment: Clear separation of transfusion medicine and transplant-team decisions; no product-release authorization.
prerequisites: Graduate-level medicine/pathology or hematology; foundational hematology, physiology, immunology, and laboratory medicine. This independent study sequence does not establish clinical eligibility.

units.title: Special populations, emergencies and clinical interfaces
objectives: Adapt consultation framing for obstetric, neonatal, sickle cell, trauma, perioperative and transplant contexts.
Use the relevant guideline population and avoid overgeneralizing trial or threshold evidence.
topics: Sickle cell transfusion/exchange and alloimmunization; HDFN/neonatal support; massive hemorrhage and component availability; perioperative/ICU; solid-organ/HSCT; pediatric considerations.
units.casePractice: Write concise case-based consult notes for two constructed specialties; state assumptions and escalation.
units.assessment: Population-specific evidence, explicit unknowns, no treatment orders or patient-specific advice.
prerequisites: Graduate-level medicine/pathology or hematology; foundational hematology, physiology, immunology, and laboratory medicine. This independent study sequence does not establish clinical eligibility.

units.title: Regulation, accreditation, informatics, research and practice improvement
objectives: Distinguish FDA guidance, regulations and professional accreditation/standards.
Design a modest, measurable transfusion quality-improvement or research question.
topics: FDA/CBER, AABB/CAP/FACT roles; quality systems and deviations; document control; hemovigilance and informatics; evidence appraisal; study design, bias and ethics; research-track limits.
units.casePractice: One-page quality-improvement proposal with measure, denominator, balancing measure and limitations.
units.assessment: Correct authority mapping, feasible measurement, privacy and ethics safeguards.
prerequisites: Graduate-level medicine/pathology or hematology; foundational hematology, physiology, immunology, and laboratory medicine. This independent study sequence does not establish clinical eligibility.

assignment.title: Transfusion-service consultation and quality review portfolio
assignment.instructions: Complete four fictional consult vignettes (compatibility/antibody, component use, reaction/hemovigilance, donor/product quality); prepare one de-identified-by-design workflow map; and propose a small quality-improvement question with numerator, denominator, balancing measure, source/version date and limitations. Do not include actual patient records or diagnostic images. Do not issue real clinical recommendations.

rubric.excellent: Shows logical differential, recognizes key alternatives and supports conclusions with current sources; uncertainty is explicit.
Identifies when local policy, transfusion-service consultation and responsible clinician review are required; no unsupervised order or release instruction.
Maps work to ABPath domains and cites authoritative versioned sources accurately.
Defines measurable process/outcome and balancing measure without causal overclaim.
Uses fictional data only, concise communication and no unauthorized images/records.

assignment.completionThreshold: Self-study benchmark only: complete each deliverable and score at least 70% against rubric; not a validated exam predictor or credential.

assessment.format: 12 unit knowledge checks; 10 original multiple-choice questions; four fictional case analyses; one final consultation/QI portfolio.
assessment.passCriterion: Suggested personal learning target: >=80% on self-authored question set after reviewing rationales, plus portfolio rubric >=70%. Not validated, not official ABPath content, and not a guarantee of board passing.
assessment.remediation: Revisit mapped primary sources, correct reasoning in writing, and reattempt using new instructor-reviewed items when available. No protected exam items are used.

studyHours.plan: 160 hours illustrative independent study: 36 hours desired lecture floor (not currently available from verified free video), 48 hours readings, 36 hours case/panel reasoning, 20 hours assessments, and 20 hours revision/QI portfolio. This is a planning estimate, not clinical training or an observed workload.

unitMap.text: Transfusion service systems, quality and consultation
coveredTopics: Laboratory and clinical interfaces; ordering and specimen identity; inventory and stewardship; emergency release; quality indicators; transfusion committee; incident learning.

unitMap.text: Blood components, preparation, storage and selection
coveredTopics: RBCs, platelets, plasma, cryoprecipitate, whole blood; leukoreduction, irradiation, washing, volume reduction, pathogen reduction; storage and transport; labeling and traceability.

unitMap.text: ABO/Rh immunohematology and genetics
coveredTopics: ABO genetics/forward-reverse typing; Rh and weak D; clinically significant antigens; dosage, phase, enzyme effects; phenotype/genotype; rare phenotypes.

unitMap.text: Pretransfusion testing and complex antibody identification
coveredTopics: Specimen identification/validity; antibody screen; panel interpretation; transfusion history; adsorption/elution; warm autoantibodies; cold interference; electronic/immediate-spin/serologic crossmatch; emergency release.

unitMap.text: RBC alloimmunization, delayed reactions and HDFN
coveredTopics: Alloantibody evanescence; delayed hemolytic/serologic reaction; DAT/elution; antigen-negative selection; anti-D prophylaxis principles; HDFN evaluation and transfusion-support concepts.

unitMap.text: Component therapy, thresholds and patient blood management
coveredTopics: RBC evidence and 2023 guideline context; platelet transfusion; plasma/coagulation; cryoprecipitate/fibrinogen; anemia and blood conservation; perioperative/ICU context; informed decision-making.

unitMap.text: Acute and delayed transfusion reactions; hemovigilance
coveredTopics: AHTR, FNHTR, allergic/anaphylactic, TACO, TRALI, TAD, septic reaction, delayed hemolytic/serologic, TA-GVHD, PTP; stop/notify/verify/investigate as local policy; severity/imputability.

unitMap.text: Transfusion-transmitted infection, donor safety and product safety
coveredTopics: Donor eligibility; testing; infectious risk mitigation; bacterial contamination of platelets; lookback/traceback; reporting; emerging pathogens; FDA guidance currency.

unitMap.text: Donor operations, collection and blood center interface
coveredTopics: Whole-blood/apheresis donation; eligibility; collection; processing; storage/distribution; donor reactions; blood center-hospital interface; supply constraints and contingency planning.

unitMap.text: Therapeutic apheresis and clinical consultation
coveredTopics: Therapeutic plasma exchange; RBC exchange; leukapheresis; photopheresis; collection vs therapeutic procedures; consultation and coordination; monitoring and adverse events.

unitMap.text: Hematopoietic transplantation, immunogenetics and cell therapy
coveredTopics: HLA matching and antibody context; HSCT support; ABO mismatch; cellular products; collection, processing, cryopreservation, release/labeling, chain of identity/custody; gene-modified therapies.

unitMap.text: Special populations, emergencies and clinical interfaces
coveredTopics: Sickle cell transfusion/exchange and alloimmunization; HDFN/neonatal support; massive hemorrhage and component availability; perioperative/ICU; solid-organ/HSCT; pediatric considerations.

unitMap.text: Regulation, accreditation, informatics, research and practice improvement
coveredTopics: FDA/CBER, AABB/CAP/FACT roles; quality systems and deviations; document control; hemovigilance and informatics; evidence appraisal; study design, bias and ethics; research-track limits.

topicGaps: 36.0 verified accessible free recording hours remain: no ledger item satisfies both observed-duration evidence and independently established unrestricted video playback for counting; 64 existing lecture entries are preserved, including two Houston Methodist items with visible related-media durations but unconfirmed playback and Hoxworth/YouTube items with unknown runtime/access evidence.

No new unique recording was appended. Ordinary public metadata attempts for the BBGuy embedded YouTube videos failed at YouTube player-response extraction; Hoxworth library entries link to YouTube but do not show runtime. Those items remain supplementary leads, not counted recordings.

Substantive residual instructional gaps remain in donor screening/testing and operations, current component evidence and thresholds, detailed immunohematology/panel work, cell therapy quality and chain-of-identity, platelet refractoriness, apheresis consultation, and population-specific practice. The newly scripted episodes address selected reasoning domains only; they do not complete the 36-hour floor.

Public Johns Hopkins and NIH program pages describe rotations and training structure, not a complete public lecture curriculum. Institution variants, clinical eligibility language, dated board status, and the distinction between programme description, board blueprint, guidance, regulation and accreditation are retained.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: American Board of Pathology (ABPath) — Blood Banking/Transfusion Medicine subspecialty certification
medical.boardStatus: A distinct ABPath Blood Banking/Transfusion Medicine subspecialty certification examination exists. ABPath currently describes a one-day computer-based exam of 280 combined written/practical one-best-answer questions in 6 hours 22 minutes. This is not a separate board exam called “Transfusion Medicine Fellowship”; certification remains ABPath subspecialty certification, subject to current eligibility rules.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Johns Hopkins states that its programme requires board eligibility in CP, AP/CP or Hematology and that successful programme completion qualifies a fellow to take the ABPath subspecialty exam. This course cannot confer eligibility. The user must verify current individualized primary-certification/training requirements and application status with ABPath; do not assume this programme page supersedes the Board.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Packet MED-136 names one Johns Hopkins clinical physician fellowship. Harvard-affiliated variants were not established in this exact item packet. NIH Clinical Center has a distinct two-year clinical GME transfusion medicine/blood banking fellowship, but it is not represented as a Harvard-affiliated or Johns Hopkins offering and is not added as an institutional variant. The curriculum draws topical context only from the public NIH page. The generic directory category is not treated as a second specialty. No research-only postdoctoral job or non-physician supplement is represented as the clinical fellowship.
sourceCaveats: Official JHU pages differ in published duration: directory says one year; department describes a one- or two-year pathway. No resolution is asserted; optional second year is described as investigative.
ABPath’s current listed final BBTM content specification is dated January 2026; re-check the Board before any application or exam preparation.
ACGME pathology requirements page lists BBTM requirements effective July 1, 2026; ACGME accreditation is not equivalent to ABPath certification.
CDC NHSN protocol v3.0 (Jan 2026) changed which categories are requested for surveillance reporting; surveillance criteria are not interchangeable with bedside diagnosis.
No source describes every proprietary or internal Johns Hopkins lecture, complete didactic schedule, case volume or clinical training hour. None is invented.
Human clinical review has not been performed. All constructed cases and practice questions are educational fictions; no real patient records or clinical images are reproduced.

No new unique recording was appended. Ordinary public metadata attempts for the BBGuy embedded YouTube videos failed at YouTube player-response extraction; Hoxworth library entries link to YouTube but do not show runtime. Those items remain supplementary leads, not counted recordings.

Substantive residual instructional gaps remain in donor screening/testing and operations, current component evidence and thresholds, detailed immunohematology/panel work, cell therapy quality and chain-of-identity, platelet refractoriness, apheresis consultation, and population-specific practice. The newly scripted episodes address selected reasoning domains only; they do not complete the 36-hour floor.

Public Johns Hopkins and NIH program pages describe rotations and training structure, not a complete public lecture curriculum. Institution variants, clinical eligibility language, dated board status, and the distinction between programme description, board blueprint, guidance, regulation and accreditation are retained.

practiceQuestions.stem: A group O patient has a newly detected anti-Jka after a prior transfusion. Which RBC selection principle is most appropriate?

options.text: Select Jka-positive units if crossmatch compatible.
Select units lacking Jka and perform compatibility testing under local policy.
Ignore anti-Jka if the current hemoglobin is low.
Issue ABO-compatible uncrossmatched cells regardless of urgency.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A clinically significant identified alloantibody should inform antigen-negative component selection; urgency and local emergency-release processes are separate decisions. This fictional item is not an order.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient develops dyspnea during transfusion. Which inference is justified from that symptom alone?

options.text: Definitive TACO.
Definitive TRALI.
A suspected reaction requiring evaluation; cause remains undetermined.
A delayed serologic reaction.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Dyspnea alone does not meet the surveillance criteria for TACO or TRALI. Assess timing, objective findings, differential diagnosis, and current institutional policy.

options.text: Within 4 hours after transfusion.
Within 12 hours after transfusion cessation.
Within 24 hours after issue.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The January 2026 NHSN v3.0 TACO definition specifies onset within 12 hours of cessation and a specified multi-criterion combination.

practiceQuestions.stem: An ABO discrepancy appears in a routine specimen, but the clinical team requests immediate RBCs. What is the best educational response?

options.text: Choose the most likely ABO group and issue without discussion.
Follow local emergency-release policy and urgently coordinate with the transfusion service while resolving the discrepancy.
Repeat the same test until it is concordant; do not communicate.
Use group AB cells for every product.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Do not guess an unresolved blood group. Emergency issue decisions require local policy, risk-benefit discussion and transfusion-service involvement.

practiceQuestions.stem: A stable adult has a hemoglobin value near a restrictive-threshold range. Which general principle best aligns with AABB 2023 guidance?

options.text: A numerical threshold automatically mandates transfusion.
Use restrictive strategy evidence for the relevant population, while considering symptoms, context and individual factors.
Transfuse to a normal laboratory reference range.
AABB discourages all RBC transfusions.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2023 guideline supports a restrictive strategy for most populations but emphasizes clinical context and signs/symptoms; the guideline is not an automatic order.

practiceQuestions.stem: A febrile reaction is reported during transfusion. What is the safest first analytic framing?

options.text: Assume FNHTR and stop workup.
Treat it as a suspected reaction, assess urgency and investigate under local protocol; exclude serious causes before a benign label.
Call it a delayed serologic reaction.
Do not examine component/unit identity.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Fever may occur in benign and serious reactions. The diagnostic and operational workup follows local policy; the question does not prescribe treatment.

title: Adolescent Medicine Fellowship
prerequisites: Advanced health-sciences learner; intended for physicians/trainees with foundational pediatrics or primary-care knowledge. It is not a substitute for MD/DO education or supervised training.
Familiarity with adolescent development, basic preventive care, interviewing and evidence appraisal.
No clinical prerequisites are checked and no learner credentials are verified.
objectives: Map learning to the 21 domains and weights in the ABP adolescent medicine content outline effective March 1, 2026.
Apply developmentally informed, trauma-sensitive and equity-aware reasoning across adolescent preventive and acute presentations.
Recognize when current guidelines, local law, supervision, specialty consultation or emergency systems are required.
Critically appraise public health evidence without confusing population prevalence, screening and diagnosis.
Explain why self-study cannot confer competence, eligibility or certification.

units.title: Development, growth, and the adolescent visit
objectives: Compare adolescent developmental tasks with normal biologic growth/puberty variation without treating age alone as maturity.
Use strengths-based, developmentally appropriate interviewing and anticipatory guidance.
Identify routine prevention and screening decisions and distinguish universal from risk-based screening.
topics: Cognitive, physical and psychosocial development
Pubertal staging, growth trajectory and confidential time
HEADSS/SSHADESS strengths-based assessment, vaccines and preventive care
units.casePractice: Use Seattle Children’s teaching vignette only as an ethics discussion (not an authentic patient case); write a fictional HEADSS history and identify what needs private time.
units.assessment: One-page structured visit plan: required elements, strengths-based opening, privacy setup and a justified screening plan.

units.title: Confidentiality, consent, privacy systems, and adolescent autonomy
objectives: Explain consent/confidentiality distinctions and limits; identify that state law, payer, EHR proxy access, portals and billing may differ.
Plan private time and confidential follow-up without promising secrecy that cannot be kept.
Escalate threats, abuse, mandatory reporting, and imminent safety concerns through locally authorized supervision.
topics: Minor consent law is service- and jurisdiction-specific
Confidentiality exceptions, assent/capacity, parent proxy access and EOB leakage
Reproductive justice, coercion avoidance and trauma-informed communication
units.casePractice: Seattle Children’s public case-based guide, including its explicit educational-use license; compare US clinic workflows and do not apply its Washington law statements elsewhere.
units.assessment: Privacy threat model for a fictional clinic encounter; five-point rubric: limits explained, private time, legal caveat, data/billing plan, escalation.

units.title: Mental health, depression, anxiety, and suicide safety
objectives: Separate screening from diagnostic assessment and treatment.
Apply age-qualified USPSTF depression recommendation accurately and state its suicide-screening I statement.
Describe an evidence-based local positive-screen pathway; distinguish ideation, attempt and NSSI.
topics: Depression screening ages 12–18; evidence is insufficient for suicide-risk screening recommendation in asymptomatic children/adolescents
ASQ is a brief screen, not risk prediction or a disposition decision; a positive screen requires further assessment
Safety planning, referral, collaborative care and urgent escalation are supervised/local functions
units.casePractice: NIMH public ASQ youth toolkit and pathways. Practice only with fictional vignettes and the official pathway; never use this course as a stand-alone crisis protocol.
units.assessment: Write a screen-to-disposition flowchart, graded for accurate USPSTF wording, second-stage assessment, imminent-risk escalation and limits.

units.title: Eating disorders, nutrition, higher weight, and medical stability
objectives: Recognize restrictive, binge/purge, avoidant/restrictive and atypical presentations without relying on appearance or BMI alone.
Interpret growth/weight trajectory, vitals and symptoms as reasons for appropriate clinician-led assessment.
Identify when acuity or medical instability warrants urgent specialty/emergency evaluation, without self-authorizing admission or treatment.
topics: Anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, binge-eating disorder, ARFID, atypical presentations
Growth charts/trajectory, orthostasis, bradycardia, electrolytes and differential diagnosis
Weight stigma, family-centered treatment and referral boundaries
units.casePractice: Use SAHM’s curriculum and published case teaching resources; source patient narrative links only, never download/rehost images or record excerpts.
units.assessment: Differential and next-step memo from a fictionalized case; rubric rewards red-flag recognition, differential, urgency, team referral and non-stigmatizing language.

units.title: Sexuality, gender, identity, and affirming communication
objectives: Use respectful, non-assumptive language and anatomy-/behavior-based history.
Differentiate sexual orientation, gender identity, expression and sex traits; avoid treating identity as pathology.
Discuss current local service scope, consent rules and referral pathways without promising access or outcomes.
topics: Developmental sexuality and psychosocial context
Gender diversity and affirmative communication
Confidential documentation, safety and intersectional health equity
units.casePractice: SAHM public curriculum links and fictional pronoun/communication role-play. SAHM Beyond the Basics lecture recordings require a free account; therefore excluded from counted hours.
units.assessment: Audio-free written encounter script plus reflection: pronouns, open questions, patient-led goals and limits.

units.title: Reproductive and contraceptive care
objectives: Elicit pregnancy-prevention goals and preferences without method steering or coercion.
Compare method attributes using current CDC U.S. SPR/MEC and patient preferences; note that the 2024 SPR is not a substitute for individual prescribing.
Identify confidential access barriers and local legal/payer issues for follow-up.

boardNames: American Board of Pediatrics (ABP) Adolescent Medicine subspecialty certification examination
American Board of Internal Medicine (ABIM) Adolescent Medicine certification pathway / joint examination
American Board of Family Medicine (ABFM) Adolescent Medicine Certificate of Added Qualification (CAQ) / joint one-day examination
medical.boardStatus: A distinct physician clinical subspecialty with a jointly developed Adolescent Medicine certification examination program (ABP, ABIM, ABFM); the ABP states it administers the exam. ABFM uses a CAQ pathway and states continuing-certification candidates transition to longitudinal assessment. Board titles/pathways and maintenance differ. This is not a generic directory category or research-only/non-physician track. The fellowship is not a combined Med-Peds residency; prior internal medicine/pediatrics residency can be an entry route. Hopkins page separately notes optional addiction medicine training and a possible separate Addiction Medicine board exam.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This course does not establish eligibility. ABP route requires primary board certification accepted by ABP, three years full-time broad-based ACGME/RCPSC-accredited adolescent-medicine fellowship training, program-director evaluation/scholarly requirements and passing the exam. ABIM’s current policy lists primary ABIM certification, 24 months fellowship including 12 clinical months, licensure/competence and passing its pathway exam. ABFM requires its separate application/eligibility review for CAQ. Confirm current policies with the board for the candidate’s primary certification and jurisdiction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A well adolescent age 15 reports no depressive symptoms and has no depression diagnosis. Which statement best matches the USPSTF recommendation?

options.text: Screen for major depressive disorder in adolescents aged 12–18; the USPSTF finds evidence insufficient for suicide-risk screening in children/adolescents.
The USPSTF recommends universal suicide-risk screening and no depression screening.
Screen only adolescents with risk factors for depression.
The recommendation covers treatment selection for diagnosed depression.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2022 USPSTF recommends MDD screening ages 12–18 (B grade) and an I statement for suicide-risk screening in children/adolescents. This recommendation applies to people without recognized symptoms/diagnosis; it does not bar assessment when concerns exist.

practiceQuestions.stem: A youth gives a positive response on the NIMH ASQ. What is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.text: The tool establishes a diagnosis and determines admission.
The screen indicates further assessment is needed; follow an appropriate clinical pathway, including a brief safety assessment by a trained clinician.
A positive screen can be disregarded if the parent denies concern.
The screen predicts an individual suicide attempt with certainty.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NIMH describes ASQ as a screen. A positive screen requires a brief suicide safety assessment and disposition using the relevant clinical pathway; it is neither diagnosis nor certain prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A clinician sees an adolescent for STI concerns. Which approach is most defensible before discussing confidentiality?

options.text: Promise that parents and insurers can never learn anything.
Explain privacy and confidentiality limits, check jurisdiction-specific consent/reporting rules, and plan EHR, portal, billing and follow-up risks.
Assume the same minor-consent law applies in every state.
Avoid discussing confidentiality because it is not clinically relevant.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Confidentiality may be affected by law, EHR access, insurance explanations of benefits, portals and clinic operations. Do not make an absolute promise or generalize one jurisdiction’s rules.
practiceQuestions.domain: 11 Ethics, Legal Issues, and Health Equity

practiceQuestions.stem: A 16-year-old asks about contraception and is unsure what matters most. Which counseling strategy best supports autonomy?

options.text: Present only the method with highest effectiveness and recommend it regardless of preference.
Elicit preferences, offer balanced information about options and trade-offs, and use shared decision-making without steering.
Ask the parent to select the method.
Withhold options that do not fit the clinician’s assumptions about the youth.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Shared decision-making centers the youth’s goals and values and considers options without coercive direction; legal consent and clinical eligibility still require current local assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about adolescent STI guidance is most accurate?

options.text: Screening should be based only on age and never on sexual exposure.
CDC guidance includes annual chlamydia and gonorrhea screening for sexually active females under 25; other screening depends on exposure, population, and guidance.
All adolescents need routine screening for every STI, including asymptomatic HSV.
Cervical cancer screening should routinely start in adolescence.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC’s published adolescent guidance supports annual chlamydia/gonorrhea screening for sexually active females under 25 and discusses exposure-based testing and other considerations. It does not recommend routine screening of asymptomatic adolescents for every STI; cervical screening starts later under cited guidelines. Recheck current guidance before practice.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which source should be used for current contraceptive practice recommendations, rather than a 2010s webinar?

options.text: A public video is always more current than a guideline.
CDC U.S. Selected Practice Recommendations for Contraceptive Use, 2024, while checking newer updates and individual eligibility.
A playlist title with no date.
A fictional case outline.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The CDC 2024 U.S. SPR is a current authoritative practice document at date checked; webinars can teach communication but should not be sole basis for current clinical decisions.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional 15-year-old has a declining growth trajectory, restrictive intake, dizziness and an abnormal resting pulse. Which next-step principle is best?

options.text: A single BMI establishes the diagnosis and can be managed with unsupervised diet advice.
Assess growth/history/vitals and medical stability promptly; arrange appropriate clinician-led urgent evaluation/referral based on findings.
Wait until the youth meets a stereotyped appearance threshold.
Assume normal labs exclude medical instability.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Eating-disorder assessment requires trajectory, history, exam/vitals and appropriate clinical evaluation; urgent instability requires supervised escalation. Appearance or a single measure is insufficient. This item is educational, not a patient-specific protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner reviews YRBS data on prevalence of adolescent substance use. Which inference is appropriate?

options.text: An aggregate survey association diagnoses an individual patient.
Public survey data describe population patterns within design limitations; they cannot establish an individual diagnosis or necessarily prove causation.
Every observed association is causal.
National high-school estimates apply to every out-of-school youth.

practiceQuestions.rationale: YRBS is a surveillance dataset useful for population patterns, not individual diagnosis; sampling, measurement, and generalizability limitations matter.

practiceQuestions.stem: A clinician plans confidential follow-up for a fictional adolescent. What is the best systems-level action?

options.text: Assume portal and billing processes preserve privacy automatically.
Make a patient-informed follow-up plan and verify local EHR proxy, contact, billing/EOB and legal processes.
Leave detailed information on the family voicemail.
Promise no one can access the medical record.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Confidentiality is affected by operational systems as well as law. The plan should be transparent, locally verified, and not overpromise privacy.
