practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly characterizes Johns Hopkins’ Adolescent Medicine Fellowship in the packet?

options.text: A generic online directory category with no physician training pathway.
A three-year ACGME-accredited clinical/research physician fellowship with clinical experiences and research training.
A research-only non-physician supplement.
A combined internal medicine/pediatrics residency.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hopkins’ official program page says Johns Hopkins Children’s Center, ACGME accredited, three years, and describes clinical plus research training. That is distinct from Med-Peds residency or a research-only position.

title: Adolescent/Young Adult Medicine Fellowship
prerequisites: Physician education and completion of an appropriate primary specialty pathway are not provided by this course. Designed as supplementary self-study for qualified trainees or clinicians with adolescent-health fundamentals.
Know basic history taking, physical examination, evidence appraisal and safeguarding escalation.
Before clinical use, learners must use current local consent, confidentiality, mandatory-reporting, STI, prescribing and referral rules.
objectives: Use developmental, family, community and life-course context to reason about health in adolescence and young adulthood.
Structure a preventive and confidential clinical encounter with explicit legal and safety boundaries.
Apply current board-domain knowledge to original cases, differentiating screen, diagnosis, risk and intervention.
Recognize when urgent assessment, supervisor input, multidisciplinary care or referral is required.
Plan transition to adult-centered care without collapsing distinct pediatric and adult approaches.
Interpret research and improve systems while identifying evidence limits and health inequities.

units.title: Development, preventive care, and the adolescent interview
objectives: Interpret physical, cognitive, and psychosocial development without treating age alone as a diagnosis.
Build a preventive visit with confidential private time, screening, strengths-based counseling, and safety-net follow-up.
topics: Pubertal timing and growth trajectory; preventive screening and immunization; HEEADSSS-style psychosocial assessment; motivational interviewing; trauma-informed and culturally responsive care.
units.casePractice: Fictional 15-year-old presents for sports clearance: prioritize private interview, targeted screening, and normal-variation versus red-flag assessment; no fabricated images.
units.assessment: Submit an annotated visit plan distinguishing universal, age-based and risk-based actions.

units.title: Confidentiality, consent, ethics, and equitable care
objectives: State confidentiality boundaries before collecting sensitive history and apply local law, mandated reporting, capacity, and safety exceptions.
Recognize EHR, proxy portal, billing, and insurance communication as confidentiality risks.
topics: Private time; minor consent statutes vary by jurisdiction/service; disclosure only as legally required/permitted; assent/capacity; EHR segmentation, portals and EOBs; disability and supported decision making; bias, racism, social determinants and equity.
boardDomains: 11 Ethics, Legal Issues, and Health Equity (3%)
units.casePractice: Role-play a minor requesting confidential sexual-health care; identify local law and safety facts to verify before promising secrecy.
units.assessment: Score a scripted visit against confidentiality, explanation, and disclosure minimization criteria.

units.title: Sexuality, gender, reproductive and sexual health
objectives: Take inclusive sexual histories based on organs, behaviors, partners, and goals, not assumptions.
Counsel on contraception, pregnancy options, consent, STI/HIV prevention and testing within current law and guidance.
topics: Gender-diverse youth affirming communication; reproductive justice; contraception including LARC; emergency contraception; pregnancy; HIV PrEP/PEP overview; STI screening by age, anatomy, exposure, site, and risk; sexual consent.
boardDomains: 11 Ethics, Legal Issues, and Health Equity (3%)
units.casePractice: Fictional 19-year-old requests STI testing: map exposed sites and anatomy, explain confidentiality/payment limitations, and select guidance questions without prescribing.
units.assessment: Write an anatomy- and exposure-based testing plan, citing current CDC pages and identifying uncertainty.

units.title: Mental and behavioral health, safety and trauma
objectives: Integrate screening with assessment and accessible treatment pathways; distinguish a screen from diagnosis.
Assess suicide/self-harm, violence, abuse, exploitation, and immediate safety while respecting legally bounded confidentiality.
topics: Depression/anxiety and integrated behavioral care; suicide risk and safety planning; trauma-informed interviewing; violence and firearm safety; bullying; homelessness; resilience and structural determinants.
boardDomains: 11 Ethics, Legal Issues, and Health Equity (3%)
units.casePractice: Fictional youth has positive mood screen and passive death wishes: use a structured safety assessment, explain disclosure boundaries, arrange timely qualified evaluation.
units.assessment: Create a referral and follow-up pathway; do not use the course as a clinical risk tool.

units.title: Substance use, addiction and harm reduction
objectives: Use an adolescent-validated universal screen and respond nonjudgmentally.
Distinguish screening from diagnosis; select brief intervention, further assessment, urgent safety response, or referral based on findings.
topics: SBIRT; S2BI/BSTAD; nicotine/vaping, alcohol, cannabis, opioids and other drugs; co-occurring mood and sleep concerns; family engagement; treatment access and harm reduction.
boardDomains: 11 Ethics, Legal Issues, and Health Equity (3%)
units.casePractice: Fictional 16-year-old reports intermittent cannabis use: practice private screening, stage-of-change conversation, risk assessment, and safe follow-up/referral.
units.assessment: Explain why a positive brief screen is not by itself a substance-use-disorder diagnosis.

units.title: Nutrition, eating disorders, obesity and food security
objectives: Recognize restrictive, binge/purge, ARFID and atypical restrictive presentations, including medical risk at any body size.
Use growth trajectory, history, physical findings, mental health and labs/ECG as indicated to determine urgency with specialist input.
topics: Growth/weight trajectory; restriction, vomiting, compulsive exercise; orthostasis and instability; malnutrition and complications; level-of-care reasoning; multidisciplinary care; family-based therapy; weight stigma, obesity, and food insecurity.
units.casePractice: Fictional teen with rapid weight loss but BMI in reference range: identify why normal BMI does not exclude medical instability and what same-day clinical assessment must establish.
units.assessment: Compare outpatient monitoring versus escalation using SAHM published criteria; do not calculate a real patient disposition.

units.title: Reproductive endocrinology, pubertal variation and gender-affirming care
objectives: Build differentials for menstrual, pubertal, endocrine and reproductive presentations, incorporating pregnancy testing when indicated and consent permits.
Discuss gender-diverse care respectfully and separate social support, mental-health support, and medical decisions requiring individualized specialist care.
topics: Amenorrhea and abnormal uterine bleeding; pubertal timing and growth; endocrine differential; menstrual health; gender-related distress and care models; consent/legal context; shared decision making.
units.casePractice: Fictional patient with amenorrhea: structure differential and initial evaluation without assuming cause from gender identity or weight.
units.assessment: Present differential with red flags and testing rationale; defer treatment decisions to clinician.

units.title: Musculoskeletal health, sports, sleep and routine conditions
objectives: Assess adolescent athletes in developmental and sport context, including injury prevention and return-to-play principles.
Apply age-specific evaluation to common dermatologic, GI, infectious, neurologic, cardiopulmonary, renal, hematologic, rheumatologic and ENT concerns.
topics: Sports participation and overuse; concussion/sleep; acne; abdominal symptoms; common infection; headaches; asthma/chest symptoms; urinary complaints; anemia; joint symptoms; evidence-based generalist scope and referral thresholds.

units.casePractice: Fictional athlete with exertional symptoms: identify immediate red flags, appropriate scope, and referral rather than issuing clearance from incomplete data.
units.assessment: Short oral case: show reasoning, uncertainty, red flags and follow-up.

units.title: Chronic illness, young-adult primary care and transition
objectives: Distinguish pediatric family-centered care from adult patient-centered care; support transition without treating transfer as a birthday event.

topics: Transfer with or without changing clinician; pediatric conditions in adult care; self-management and decision support; medication reconciliation; adult preventive care; disability and capacity supports; coverage and continuity.
boardDomains: 21 Head, Eye, Ear, Nose, and Throat (2%)
units.casePractice: Fictional 20-year-old with congenital heart disease has missed appointments: map each transition element and identify which pediatric team/adult clinician owns the next action.
units.assessment: Design a transition plan with measurable completion rather than merely referral.

objectives: Design a focused scholarly question and evaluate evidence quality, bias, and applicability.

topics: Youth engagement; community outreach; advocacy; health disparities and structural racism; research ethics; study design, critical appraisal, statistics basics; QI; teaching and feedback.
boardDomains: 11 Ethics, Legal Issues, and Health Equity (3%)
units.casePractice: Fictional clinic discovers confidential-result failures: define process measure, population, balancing measure, and youth-informed improvement strategy.

units.title: Inpatient adolescent medicine and integrated care
objectives: Use a structured approach to admitting presentations such as restrictive eating complications, abnormal uterine bleeding, and acute safety concerns.

objectives: Use the official ABP 2026 adolescent medicine outline to map study needs without treating it as a full curriculum.
Interpret research claims and separate screening, diagnosis, and intervention evidence.

units.casePractice: Sort original practice questions by domain and explain why each distractor is less appropriate.

assignment: Complete one domain-tagged case portfolio, a reflective confidentiality role-play, a source-graded clinical reasoning brief, and a transition-process map. Use fictional cases only. Obtain qualified supervision for any clinical activity. The assignments are not a validated exam predictor.

assessment.formative: 10 original single-best-answer questions with rationales, oral case summaries, self-assessment by ABP domain, and reflective assignments.
assessment.summative: Domain portfolio, critical-appraisal brief, simulated handoff, and learner self-audit against the published outline. No pass threshold is claimed to predict certification.
assessment.limits: Questions are independently written for this course, not released board items; assessment has not been psychometrically validated and cannot establish competency, readiness, board eligibility or certification.

studyHours.timeBudget: Suggested self-study plan: 36 hours of video at the course target (only 1.7114 verified now; the remaining 34.2886 hours are not yet produced), 44 hours reading and guideline reconciliation, 30 hours case-based reasoning and assignment work, 12 hours retrieval practice and review, and 10 hours scholarship/quality-improvement application. This is a study plan, not the real duration of fellowship and not a claim that future media exist.

medical.boardStatus: Adolescent medicine has a distinct subspecialty certification pathway jointly established by ABP, ABIM, and ABFM; board-specific eligibility and primary-board routes differ. This is not a generic “adolescent medicine board” invented by the course.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: ABP reports that its applicants must hold ABP pediatrics, ABIM internal medicine, or ABFM family medicine certification and complete three years of full-time broad-based fellowship in ACGME-accredited US or RCPSC-accredited Canadian adolescent medicine training, plus program-director evaluation, scholarly activity criteria and the exam. ABP advises candidates with ABIM/ABFM primary certificates to contact their primary board for eligibility. Boston Children’s public pages describe three years for pediatric-trained physicians and an opportunity for two years after prior internal/family medicine training; this institutional statement is not silently equated with ABP’s candidate requirements. Confirm accreditation and current pathways with the programme and relevant board.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Only the supplied Boston Children’s official programme variant was included. Public descriptions, individual board criteria and ABP examination content outline are distinct source types. Program pages do not disclose all lectures, case counts, assessment systems or exact didactic hours.
sourceCaveats: Boston Children’s public training pages do not publish a complete lecture list or exact didactic hour total. Rotation descriptions were observed but do not establish clinical volume or equivalence.

The programme’s duration statement for non-pediatric applicants and ABP’s three-year eligibility rule are preserved separately. ABIM/ABFM primary-board-specific routes require verification with each board.

The ABP outline effective March 1, 2026 lists 21 domains and approximate exam weights but states it is not a curriculum or study guide. Unit-to-domain mapping is instructional, not official endorsement.
The SAHM public recording catalogue describes hour-long lectures but gates video access behind portal login. Those inaccessible items are uncounted.
Observed public video player time is not permission to download, embed, or rehost media. The course links out.
All constructed cases are fictional. Generated visuals may be conceptual only. No real diagnostic image, patient record, treatment dose, or clinical authorization is included.
Current local law and guidelines can change. Verify before any clinical use. No human clinician has reviewed this course.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 16-year-old arrives with a parent for a routine visit. Which opening best supports confidential adolescent care?

options.text: Ask the parent to leave without explanation.
Explain that private time is a routine part of adolescent visits, describe confidentiality and limits, then invite questions.
Promise that nothing can ever be shared.
Conduct all sensitive screening with the parent present.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAP recommends consistent private time and an honest explanation of limits; confidentiality varies with law and circumstance.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient asks whether a parent can view a sensitive result through a portal. What is the best first response?

options.text: Guarantee that portal access is impossible.
Explain what the clinician knows, review clinic-approved confidentiality workflows, and check applicable law and account access.
Delete the result from the chart.
Tell the patient to use someone else’s account.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAP identifies proxy portal and EHR data flow as system confidentiality issues; do not promise more than law and workflow support.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 15-year-old has a positive brief substance-use screen. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: The screen establishes a substance use disorder.
The screen is a starting point for a nonjudgmental, developmentally appropriate assessment.
A parent must always be notified immediately.
No follow-up is needed if use is intermittent.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NIDA describes brief adolescent screening tools as part of SBIRT; positive responses call for further assessment and appropriate follow-up.

practiceQuestions.stem: A young person with restrictive eating has substantial recent weight loss but a BMI within the population reference range. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Medical risk is excluded.
Weight trajectory, vital signs, symptoms, behavior, exam and clinical context still need assessment.
Hospitalize solely because of the report.
BMI determines whether an eating disorder is present.

practiceQuestions.rationale: SAHM emphasizes assessment of trajectory and medical complications; normal or higher weight does not exclude need for stabilization.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is a factor SAHM identifies as supporting hospitalization consideration for restrictive eating disorders?

options.text: A single missed school day.
Electrolyte disturbance or physiologic instability.
A specific body shape.
A positive screening score alone.

practiceQuestions.rationale: SAHM published factors include electrolyte disturbance, ECG abnormalities, physiologic instability and other acute risks; decisions require comprehensive clinical assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A clinic refers a 20-year-old with a chronic condition to an adult specialist. Which action best demonstrates transition completion?

options.text: Referral placed.
Records faxed.
Confirm first adult visit occurred, continuity needs were reconciled, and the young adult knows how to access care.
Close the chart at age 18.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Got Transition’s six elements include transition completion and feedback; a referral alone is not closed-loop integration.

practiceQuestions.stem: A transgender adolescent requests STI screening. What is the most appropriate screening frame?

options.text: Screen only based on gender label.
Ask respectfully about relevant anatomy, sexual practices and exposures; select sites and tests using current recommendations.
Avoid screening because guidance is uncertain.
Use the same tests for all patients regardless of exposure.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC advises adapting screening by anatomy and considering exposure-specific sites; the history should be respectful and individualized.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the most appropriate distinction between the ABP content outline and this course?

options.text: The ABP outline is the official complete curriculum.
The ABP outline is an exam blueprint and explicitly is not a curriculum or study guide.
The outline guarantees exam success.
The outline replaces fellowship requirements.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABP says the outline maps likely exam domains/weights and is not intended as curriculum or study guide.

practiceQuestions.stem: A school athlete reports exertional chest symptoms during clearance. What is an appropriate educational response?

options.text: Clear the athlete using this course’s checklist.
Recognize the potential red flag and arrange evaluation within supervised clinical and institutional pathways.
Assume anxiety without assessment.
Issue a return-to-play decision remotely.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The curriculum teaches scope, red flags and referral, not independent clearance; evaluation requires clinician assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which interpretation of the Boston Children’s public fellowship pages is justified?

options.text: They disclose every lecture and exact didactic hour.
They describe selected public rotations and experiences, not the complete private curriculum or all required clinical volume.
They establish board eligibility for all candidate backgrounds.
They prove this self-study course is equivalent to fellowship.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The hospital publishes rotation descriptions; its pages do not disclose the complete curriculum, and board-specific eligibility is separate.

title: Boston Combined Residency Program (Pediatrics)
prerequisites: Designed for advanced learners who already have medical-school-level biomedical and clinical foundations; it is not a pathway into medical school or residency.
Expected foundations: physiology, pathology, pharmacology, epidemiology, developmental science, evidence appraisal, and clinical communication.
Read current ABP blueprint and consult up-to-date CDC/AAP/NIH guidance. Practice questions are original educational items, not official ABP content.
Do not use this independent course to diagnose, treat, prescribe, perform procedures, claim clinical experience, or access/submit identifiable patient information.
objectives: Map study across all 24 ABP General Pediatrics blueprint domains and four universal tasks while distinguishing a board blueprint from institutional curricula and ACGME requirements.
Organize age-aware pediatric problems with differential diagnosis, urgency, evidence limitations, shared decision-making, and appropriate escalation.
Explain how developmental surveillance, validated screening, assessment and referral differ.
Use current sources for changing recommendations (including immunization and newborn jaundice) rather than relying on memorized stale thresholds.
Recognize child safety, psychosocial, ethical, equity and QI dimensions within pediatric reasoning.
Respect limits: self-study cannot provide supervised competence, training credits, licensure, accreditation or board eligibility.

assignment.title: Integrated fictional case portfolio (five short exercises)
assignment.instructions: Submit five text-only, explicitly fictional pediatric vignettes: (1) well-visit/development, (2) newborn transition/jaundice, (3) adolescent psychosocial assessment, (4) acute febrile/respiratory presentation, and (5) cross-cutting safety/QI reflection. For each, state what is known, what is missing, a short differential, the source date, and the next supervised clinical or referral step. Do not insert identifiable information, real images, treatment orders or copied board questions.

rubric.criterion: Differential, risk and next information needed
Current source quality/date and correct application
Family-centered communication, equity and ethical limitations

assignment.passRule: Formative only; no validated pass standard or prediction of clinical competence.

components: 12 unit retrieval checks and case-practice exercises
assessment.scoringNote: Any suggested scoring is educational only. No exam items are copied from ABP or other boards; performance is not a valid predictor of ABP examination outcome or safe clinical practice.

studyHours.allocation: 12 units × 8–12 hours, approximately 120 hours total for reading, note-making, case discussion and retrieval practice; this is a proposed workload, not observed course duration or residency training time. Video hours are tracked separately.

mapping.institution: Boston Children’s Hospital and Boston Medical Center
mapping.name: Boston Combined Residency Program (Pediatrics) — Categorical Track

The categorical track emphasizes academic/general and subspecialty pediatrics, reports approximately 80% of training at BCH and 20% at BMC, and is a three-year program in the public description. All residents receive broad pediatrics training. Public pages describe aims, tracks and rotations but do not provide complete rotation schedules, case logs or a full accessible didactic/video curriculum.

Separate NRMP track identifier 1259320C1. Not a separate physician specialty or separate ABP exam.

topicGaps: Verified ledger totals 6.663333 of the 36 requested video hours; 29.336667 hours remain. Seven recordings added. Existing L01 and L02 remain duration-unknown and excluded.

The ABP outline spans 24 domains; verified videos are concentrated in neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, DKA evidence appraisal, pulmonary hypertension, nephrotic-syndrome evidence generation, older vaccine/RSV prevention talks, and adolescent eating disorders. Recorded coverage remains insufficient for most domain-level objectives.

No verified full-length recordings were found in this pass to establish adequate topic coverage for orthopedics/sports medicine, rheumatology, neurology, dermatology, hematology-oncology, allergy/immunology, gastroenterology, GU, genetics/metabolism, child protection, ethics, QI/research methods, and many preventive/adolescent domains.

The vaccine lecture (2022) and RSV lecture (2023) are historical and cannot be used as current schedules/product recommendations; pair with dated official CDC/AAP/FDA sources. Current guidance must be rechecked.
BCRP public descriptions do not disclose full schedules, complete didactics, case logs or video curricula; this course does not claim to reproduce the institutional curriculum.

The remaining observed-hours deficit cannot be met by the authored episodes or planned production minutes. Do not treat target minutes as rendered hours; full 36-hour feasibility remains unestablished.

boardNames: American Board of Pediatrics (ABP) — General Pediatrics

boardStatus.primaryBoard: American Board of Pediatrics (ABP), General Pediatrics
boardStatus.status: The ABP publishes a General Pediatrics initial certifying examination and a corresponding public content outline, which also applies to ITE, MOC and MOCA-Peds assessments. This is a physician board certification pathway, distinct from ACGME programme accreditation and local BCRP curriculum.
boardStatus.separateBoardExam: Yes: ABP General Pediatrics initial certifying examination exists. No separate ABP board exam is associated merely with the Categorical or LEAD BCRP tracks. BCRP combined programmes have additional discipline-specific certification pathways; their exact requirements are set by each other certifying board and are outside this general-pediatrics curriculum.
boardStatus.blueprintScope: ABP 2024 General Pediatrics Content Outline (effective for exams from Oct 15, 2024; minor revisions Dec 2024): 24 domains weighted from Preventive Pediatrics/Well-Child Care (12%) to Genetics/Dysmorphology/Metabolic Disorders (2%), Rheumatology (2%), Ethics (2%), and Patient Safety/Quality Improvement/Research Methods (2%). Four universal tasks: physiology/pathophysiology; epidemiology/risk assessment; diagnosis; management/treatment. See official outline; mappings in this course are study aids, not exam predictions.
boardStatus.eligibilitySummary: ABP admission requires an eligible medical-school degree, satisfactory completion of full accredited pediatric residency (three years for ACGME; four years for RCPSC under rules effective Jan 2025), qualifying unrestricted U.S./Canada license, and programme-director verification; consult ABP for current rule text and individual determination.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent self-study course confers no medical degree, ACGME/RCPSC training credit, supervised clinical experience or case volume, ABP or other board eligibility, license, clinical competence, credential, accreditation, or likelihood of passing. ABP and other boards determine eligibility under their current rules. It grants no institutional affiliation, and it cannot replace accredited residency or supervised care.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The packet’s named programme is a genuine clinical physician pediatrics residency, jointly based at Boston Children’s Hospital and Boston Medical Center; it is neither a generic directory category, research-only postdoctoral role, nor non-physician supplement. Exact categorical and LEAD tracks and the distinct BCRP-linked Pediatrics–Anesthesiology, Pediatrics–Medical Genetics, and two separately site/track-identified Pediatrics–Child Neurology pathways are preserved. BCRP also identifies a BCH–Tufts Triple Board program and an associated BWH/BCH Med-Peds program; these are related but distinct combined programmes, not silently collapsed into the core general-pediatrics course. No research pathway is represented as a different physician specialty or board. No non-physician supplement applies. BCRP’s public curriculum explains aims and governance but not the full institutional syllabus, lectures, schedules, or case volumes. Current official programme pages and board rules can change.
sourceCaveats: BCRP pages are official institutional descriptions, not the actual full syllabus or proof of any individual’s eligibility or training completion.
ACGME requirements are accreditation standards, not a board examination blueprint or local rotation schedule.
The ABP outline describes exam scope/weights; it is not a guarantee of any examination’s exact content or pass outcome.

Clinical guidance changes. AAP indicates the 2022 hyperbilirubinemia guidance applies through August 2027 for infants ≥35 weeks; verify updates after that date and all current schedules at point of learning.
CHOP OPEN course is free but registration-gated for viewing; its public page does not expose lecture duration. Free access does not grant reuse rights.
Stanford grand rounds are broad scholarly material; a public playlist/title alone does not establish a complete curriculum, clinical guidance currency, or runtime.
No counted video hours; individual YouTube runtimes were not verified after metadata request timed out. Unknown time remains unknown, not estimated.

Case resources are links only. No clinical photographs, patient records, screenshots or third-party assets have been copied. HRSA’s former RUSP page notes that its committee was terminated in March 2025 and the page is archival; use current state newborn-screening program resources and HRSA’s current Newborn Screening Information Center instead.

Recorded coverage remains insufficient for most domain-level objectives.

No verified full-length recordings were found in this pass to establish adequate topic coverage for orthopedics/sports medicine, rheumatology, neurology, dermatology, hematology-oncology, allergy/immunology, gastroenterology, GU, genetics/metabolism, child protection, ethics, QI/research methods, and many preventive/adolescent domains.

BCRP public descriptions do not disclose full schedules, complete didactics, case logs or video curricula; this course does not claim to reproduce the institutional curriculum.

practiceQuestions.stem: At a routine visit, a parent reports concern about a toddler’s language progress. Which approach best distinguishes developmental surveillance from screening?

options.text: A milestone checklist alone establishes or excludes a developmental disorder.
Ongoing family-informed surveillance is complemented by an age-appropriate validated screen and referral/evaluation when indicated.
Wait until school entry because early concerns are not actionable.
Use a single milestone item as a diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC distinguishes ongoing developmental surveillance from standardized developmental screening; neither a checklist nor a screen alone is a definitive diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A newborn’s bilirubin is being assessed for a learning exercise. Which information is essential before applying a current AAP treatment/follow-up framework?

options.text: Only the infant’s skin color.
Gestational age, age in hours, measured bilirubin and relevant neurotoxicity risk factors.
Birthweight alone.
A visual estimate with no timing.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAP guidance is designed for infants ≥35 weeks and uses age-specific assessment, gestation and risk; this educational question does not provide a treatment threshold or clinical order.

practiceQuestions.stem: A clinician is asked whether a late immunization dose invalidates all prior doses. What is the safest board-style next step?

options.text: Restart every vaccine series automatically.
Consult the current CDC/AAP schedule and catch-up guidance, accounting for product and interval rules.
Assume all delayed vaccines are contraindicated.
Use the schedule remembered from medical school.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Timing and spacing rules are vaccine- and age-specific and may change; use the current official schedule and general best practices.

practiceQuestions.stem: A school-age child has episodic wheeze. Which reasoning best supports an evidence-based asthma discussion?

options.text: A single episode always proves persistent asthma.
Integrate history, objective assessment when feasible, severity/control and current guideline recommendations; consider alternatives.
Use a treatment recommendation from an undated social-media post.
Ignore response pattern and triggers.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NHLBI guidance supports structured assessment and shared decision-making; an individual course cannot prescribe or replace clinician assessment.

practiceQuestions.stem: A febrile child has tachycardia and poor perfusion in a fictional vignette. Which initial cognitive priority is most appropriate?

options.text: Complete a long outpatient differential before evaluating stability.
Recognize possible shock, rapidly assess ABCs and mental status, and activate appropriate supervised emergency response.
Assume dehydration without reassessment.
Wait for a single laboratory result before escalating.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Emergency/critical care reasoning prioritizes immediate threats and stabilization; this is a cognitive safety principle, not an unsupervised protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adolescent asks to speak without a caregiver present. Which response is best?

options.text: Refuse; confidentiality never applies to minors.
Explain privacy and its limits, invite a private developmentally appropriate discussion, and follow jurisdictional safety/reporting obligations.
Promise absolute secrecy under every circumstance.
Discuss sensitive history only with the caregiver.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Adolescent care requires developmentally appropriate confidentiality while explaining exceptions and applicable local law/safety limits.

practiceQuestions.stem: A screening questionnaire for depression is positive. What conclusion is justified?

options.text: The questionnaire alone proves a psychiatric diagnosis.
A positive screen signals need for appropriate clinical assessment, safety evaluation and follow-up; it is not by itself a diagnosis.
No further action is needed if the adolescent appears calm.
The result should be ignored unless a parent confirms it.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Screening identifies possible risk and must be followed by appropriate assessment and systems for diagnosis, treatment or referral.

practiceQuestions.stem: An infant’s newborn screening result is reported as abnormal. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: A screening result is a confirmed diagnosis.
Promptly follow the state newborn screening program’s confirmatory/referral instructions; screening is not diagnosis.
Repeat the test at the next annual checkup.
Do not inform the family until symptoms emerge.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Newborn screening aims to detect conditions early but abnormal screens need timely follow-up/confirmatory assessment through the responsible program.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has a limp and fever in a fictional case stem. Which approach best demonstrates sound reasoning?

options.text: Assume a sports strain without examination.
Treat fever, inability to bear weight, joint findings and age as urgency/differential clues and identify need for prompt supervised evaluation.
Use imaging as the only data point.
Conclude juvenile arthritis from one symptom.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Pediatric limp has broad causes; systemic symptoms and function change affect urgency. A vignette cannot replace real examination or diagnostic testing.

practiceQuestions.stem: A team wants to improve developmental referral completion. Which first QI measure is most appropriate?

options.text: Define a process/outcome measure and a baseline with a clear denominator before testing a small workflow change.
Claim success after one anecdote.
Change multiple processes at once without measurement.
Use a raw count without defining eligible visits.

practiceQuestions.rationale: QI requires a defined aim and measures with denominators/baseline to understand process change; local patient-safety governance applies.

title: Child and Adolescent Psychiatry Fellowship

prerequisites.level: Advanced self-study, intended for licensed physicians or learners with foundational medical/psychiatric training; patient-care decisions require qualified clinical supervision.
requiredKnowledge: Basic neuroscience, psychiatric interviewing and mental status examination
Evidence appraisal and clinical ethics foundations
prerequisites.sequence: Complete developmental formulation and evaluation before topic disorder modules; complete assessment and safety modules before psychopharmacology, psychotherapy or systems application.
prerequisites.limitations: No supervised patient contact, procedures, case logs, rotations, credentialing, clinical skills verification, licensure or board eligibility.

objectives: Construct developmentally informed biopsychosocial and culturally responsive formulations from multiple information sources.
Generate and prioritize differential diagnoses across neurodevelopmental, mood, anxiety, trauma, disruptive, substance-use, eating, sleep, somatic and neurologic presentations.
Select appropriate assessment questions, collateral sources and validated instrument considerations while respecting limits of screening.
Explain evidence-informed treatment principles, shared decision-making and medication safety without offering patient-specific orders.
Describe emergency risk-response pathways and appropriately escalate imminent safety concerns.
Analyze consultation, school, forensic, community and health-system interfaces including ethics and confidentiality.

boardNames: American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology (ABPN) — Child and Adolescent Psychiatry subspecialty certification examination
medical.boardStatus: Separate ABPN subspecialty certification exam exists. ABPN states applicants must hold Psychiatry certification by the deadline, complete two full years (24 calendar months) of CAP subspecialty training in qualifying accredited programmes (with defined exceptional pathways and detailed rules), meet clinical skills evaluation and license conditions. Programme-specific accreditation/eligibility was not independently verified for both packet-listed sites; consult current ABPN requirements and ACGME directory.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent self-study course confers no ABPN eligibility. ABPN requirements are date-sensitive; as checked 2026-10-07, ABPN describes CAP as a psychiatry subspecialty, requires Psychiatry certification by the year before the CAP exam and two full years of CAP training subject to published detailed rules, plus clinical skills evaluations and unrestricted license. Verify exact individual eligibility directly with ABPN and the programme.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Packet establishes two included official physician fellowship offerings. Johns Hopkins is a named clinical fellowship. CHA is a named clinical fellowship and Harvard Medical School affiliated training site. Harvard HMS publicly also lists distinct site curricula at Boston Children’s Hospital and MGH/McLean; they are acknowledged as separate institutional variants but not silently added as packet variants. Not a research-only postdoctoral fellowship or non-physician category. Current accreditation for each individual program not conclusively verified in this task; CHA reports historical ACGME certification (1967), while Johns Hopkins general directory category is not equivalent to a current individual program-status determination.
sourceCaveats: ABPN and ACGME are primary authorities for certification and accredited educational requirements; a university fellowship page alone does not establish current board eligibility.
ABPN CAP blueprint posted March 2026 was used. The ABPN page also showed time-sensitive 2026 exam dates; applicants must verify later schedules and current application rules.
AACAP marks prior Practice Parameters discontinued and ordinarily outdated after five years; use current guideline series and update checks rather than treating legacy documents as current standards.
Clinical practice requires review of current guidelines, product labeling and local law; the course is self-study only.
Search result and direct runtime probes did not establish full-length free-access runtimes for lecture candidates; no candidate counted toward observed hours.
Clinical images and private patient records are not included, downloaded or copied. Free-to-view is not rights to rehost.
No human clinical review performed.

practiceQuestions.stem: A school screening questionnaire is above threshold for possible autism in a preschool child. What is the most defensible next interpretation?

options.text: The screening result confirms autism.
It signals need for clinical developmental assessment; screening alone is not diagnostic.
Repeat the same screener until a negative result.
Begin disorder-specific medication.

practiceQuestions.rationale: CDC distinguishes screening from a formal diagnostic evaluation using developmental history/behavior and trained assessment.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABPN D1-01, D2-B/C/D/F/G; ACGME evaluation/formulation milestones

practiceQuestions.stem: A fellow receives conflicting parent and teacher accounts of inattention. What should the formulation do first?

options.text: Average their scores and call it ADHD.
Record each source, context and impairment, then seek developmentally and setting-appropriate clarification.
Ignore teacher data.
Assume willful noncompliance.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Multi-informant data must be interpreted in context; AAP ADHD guidance supports evaluating symptoms/impairment across settings, while ACGME milestones include collateral integration.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adolescent endorses suicidal thoughts on a screen during a clinic visit. Which is the safest educational principle?

options.text: The screen alone determines disposition.
Ignore it if mood appears calm.
Treat it as a prompt for a qualified clinical risk assessment and follow local urgent safety procedures.
Promise absolute confidentiality.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has chronic irritability without clearly established discrete episodes of elevated mood. What reasoning is strongest?

options.text: Irritability alone proves bipolar disorder.

Exclude mood disorders because the patient is young.
Use medication response to make diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPN blueprint includes depressive, bipolar and disruptive mood conditions; longitudinal pattern and differential matter; avoid single-feature diagnostic certainty.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is a core feature of a developmentally sensitive psychiatric evaluation?

options.text: Rely only on the child’s first answer.
Integrate history, mental status and relevant collateral, considering developmental and family context.
Use an adult interview unchanged for all ages.
Replace clinical assessment with rating scales.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPN and ACGME assessment frameworks include developmentally appropriate interview, collateral and formulation.

practiceQuestions.stem: A caregiver asks for an individualized medication dose based on a course video. What should learner do?

options.text: Provide a dose from memory.
Explain that course material is not individual prescribing advice and direct to treating clinician with current prescribing references.
Recommend doubling the dose.
Use a peer’s regimen.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the meaning of ACGME CAP Milestones 2.0?

options.text: They are a standalone certification exam blueprint.

assignment.title: Integrated fictional case conference and dual-blueprint map

rubric: 20% accurate problem representation and developmental context

assignment.limitation: Formative education only; rubric is not validated, not clinical credentialing and not a proxy for board performance.

assessment.formative: 12 unit case memos, 10 original practice questions, cumulative fictional oral handoff and self-audit against ABP/ABA blueprints. Review missed concepts against current primary sources.
assessment.summative: Self-study capstone scored with assignment rubric; no pass certificate or eligibility determination.
assessment.validityNotice: Questions are original practice items, not official board questions, validated psychometric items or a board-passing predictor.

studyHours.basis: Transparent self-study schedule: 12 units × 10 hours (120 h); 36–72 h video review as video inventory grows; 20 h assignments/case synthesis; 8 h spaced retrieval and self-checks. These are learner planning allocations, not observed media duration and not residency time.

topicGaps: The publicly indexed playlist/channel sample is not a full blueprint course; long-form general pediatrics across preventive care, development, adolescent health, GI, endocrine, infectious disease, hematology/oncology, renal and primary care remains underrepresented.
Anesthesiology needs additional foundation, subspecialty, pharmacology, equipment, obstetric, neuro, regional, critical care and applied-exam media.
Pediatric anesthesia current guidelines, neonatal/infant-specific board-level media and high-quality clinical playback accessibility need individual review.
The 60+ hour aggregate target shortfall is genuine and not filled by planned scripts.
The 36-hour component floors remain unmet: verified anesthesiology-only and pediatrics-only recording time is reported separately; pediatric-anesthesia-specific hours are not double-credited.

Public lectures add meaningful coverage in obstetric anesthesia, EEG/monitoring, regional pain-risk reasoning, crisis-resource management, preschool wheeze, adolescent eating disorders and preterm growth, but do not approximate complete ABP or ABA blueprint coverage.

Still insufficiently covered by sourced long-form media: general pediatric preventive and ambulatory medicine, adolescent health breadth, GI, endocrine, infectious disease, renal, hematology/oncology, neurology, developmental-behavioral pediatrics, and pediatric congenital cardiac disease.

Still insufficiently covered by sourced long-form media: anesthetic basic sciences, pharmacology, workstation/equipment, obstetric and neuroanesthesia depth, cardiac/thoracic anesthesia, critical care, transfusion/coagulation, APPLIED oral/written examination skills, and current pediatric-specific perioperative guidelines.

Playback/caption availability and clinical currency were not individually audited by streaming all recordings; the dated Norton adolescent recording explicitly had an expired CME term. Check current guidelines before learning clinical decisions.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: American Board of Pediatrics (ABP) — General Pediatrics Initial Certifying Examination
American Board of Anesthesiology (ABA) — BASIC, ADVANCED and APPLIED examinations
medical.boardStatus: Distinct board certification routes exist for general pediatrics (ABP) and anesthesiology (ABA). The combined program is not a separate board or combined examination. Completion of approved combined training may satisfy training requirements for each board; actual eligibility is determined by each board’s current rules. Johns Hopkins identifies the five-year program as ACGME Accredited. The current ACGME directory page lists the Anesthesiology-Pediatrics combined specialty; the public ADS finder required dynamic session interaction and did not provide a program-specific record in the stateless review.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent course does not create board eligibility. The ABP says a Pediatrics-Anesthesiology applicant must complete joint training in an integrated ACGME-accredited program and may not take the ABP certifying exam until all training in both programs is complete. The ABA separately administers BASIC, ADVANCED and APPLIED examination components. Confirm current requirements directly with ABP, ABA, ACGME and the program.

topicGaps: The publicly indexed playlist/channel sample is not a full blueprint course; long-form general pediatrics across preventive care, development, adolescent health, GI, endocrine, infectious disease, hematology/oncology, renal and primary care remains underrepresented.
Anesthesiology needs additional foundation, subspecialty, pharmacology, equipment, obstetric, neuro, regional, critical care and applied-exam media.
Pediatric anesthesia current guidelines, neonatal/infant-specific board-level media and high-quality clinical playback accessibility need individual review.
The 60+ hour aggregate target shortfall is genuine and not filled by planned scripts.
The 36-hour component floors remain unmet: verified anesthesiology-only and pediatrics-only recording time is reported separately; pediatric-anesthesia-specific hours are not double-credited.

Public lectures add meaningful coverage in obstetric anesthesia, EEG/monitoring, regional pain-risk reasoning, crisis-resource management, preschool wheeze, adolescent eating disorders and preterm growth, but do not approximate complete ABP or ABA blueprint coverage.

Still insufficiently covered by sourced long-form media: general pediatric preventive and ambulatory medicine, adolescent health breadth, GI, endocrine, infectious disease, renal, hematology/oncology, neurology, developmental-behavioral pediatrics, and pediatric congenital cardiac disease.

Still insufficiently covered by sourced long-form media: anesthetic basic sciences, pharmacology, workstation/equipment, obstetric and neuroanesthesia depth, cardiac/thoracic anesthesia, critical care, transfusion/coagulation, APPLIED oral/written examination skills, and current pediatric-specific perioperative guidelines.

Playback/caption availability and clinical currency were not individually audited by streaming all recordings; the dated Norton adolescent recording explicitly had an expired CME term. Check current guidelines before learning clinical decisions.

practiceQuestions.stem: In a simulated pediatric induction, a trainee proposes using an adult airway plan unchanged for a small infant. Which principle best supports adapting the plan?

options.text: Age-related anatomy and physiology alter airway dimensions, oxygen reserve and failure tolerance.
Children and adults have identical airway dimensions when weight is similar.
One adult-sized airway plan is sufficient regardless of age.
A normal prior anesthetic eliminates present airway risk.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Age-related anatomy and physiology alter airway dimensions, oxygen reserve and failure tolerance. Distractors are intentionally unsafe generalizations; use the source-linked current institutional/board guidance for real care. This original educational item is not an official board question or a validated predictor.

title: Combined Pediatrics and Medical Genetics Residency
level: Clinical physician residency — an integrated combined residency in general pediatrics and Clinical Genetics and Genomics; not a research-only appointment, lab fellowship, genetic-counseling programme or generic directory label.-aligned independent study

prerequisites.level: Post-MD/DO educational self-study for clinicians or advanced trainees; it is not an entry medical curriculum.
priorKnowledge: General pediatrics and internal medicine foundations
Human genetics, cell biology, molecular biology and biochemistry
Basic evidence appraisal, clinical communication and ethics
prerequisites.accessNote: Applicants to actual training must consult the programme/ERAS and both boards for current degree, training, application and eligibility requirements.

objectives: Reason through a pediatric genetics referral using structured phenotype, history, pedigree and differential diagnosis.
Select testing strategies based on the clinical question, variant mechanism, test capability/limitations, family values and up-to-date guidance.
Interpret classification terminology, segregation, gene–disease validity and uncertainty without treating a VUS as a diagnosis.
Explain newborn screening as a public-health signal requiring jurisdiction-specific follow-up and confirmatory assessment.
Integrate genetics with pediatric acute care, development, newborn, adolescent, neurologic, metabolic, cardiovascular and multisystem domains.
Communicate consent, secondary findings, uncertainty, family implications and referral needs respectfully.
Map learning domains to separate ABP general pediatrics and ABMGG clinical genetics competencies without implying a combined joint exam or eligibility.
Identify the boundaries of a nonclinical self-study curriculum and the need for supervised accredited training.

units.title: Foundations: human variation, inheritance and clinical genetics
prerequisites: Medical degree-level biology; basic cell biology and biochemistry.
objectives: Explain Mendelian, mitochondrial, chromosomal and multifactorial inheritance while accounting for penetrance, expressivity, mosaicism and de novo variation.
Construct a three-generation pedigree and use it to revise—not dictate—a differential diagnosis.
Distinguish a phenotype hypothesis from a molecular diagnosis and state the limits of recurrence-risk estimates.
topics: Pedigrees and segregation
Variant classes and mechanisms
Penetrance/expressivity
Phenotype-first reasoning
Bayesian thinking and ascertainment
boardDomains: ABMGG: basic genetics, inheritance, genomic medicine, clinical assessment
units.casePractice: Fictional three-generation pedigree with apparently unaffected transmitting relatives; list competing inheritance models.
units.assessment: Pedigree interpretation; rubric: inheritance model 30%, uncertainty/alternative explanations 30%, accurate family communication 20%, documentation 20%.

units.title: Clinical genetics encounter, dysmorphology and phenotype encoding
prerequisites: Unit 1.
objectives: Obtain an age-appropriate prenatal, birth, developmental, medical and family history relevant to suspected genetic disease.
Perform a structured systems review and use standardized phenotype terms to describe findings without premature syndrome labeling.
Prioritize safety-critical findings and coordinate consultations/referrals.
topics: Dysmorphology approach
Growth parameters and head circumference
Developmental history
Phenotype ontologies and HPO-style terms
Medical records and data quality
boardDomains: ABP: growth and development; newborn care
units.casePractice: Use an openly curated ClinGen/ClinVar resource only as a learning datum; learner case itself is fictional.
units.assessment: Phenotype-to-differential note; rubric: precise observed features 35%, prioritized differential 25%, testable next steps 25%, respectful language 15%.

units.title: Newborn screening, biochemical genetics and time-critical follow-up
prerequisites: Units 1–2; introductory metabolism.
objectives: Explain the difference between population screening, confirmatory diagnosis and diagnostic testing.
For an abnormal screen, identify immediate escalation and confirmatory-testing principles without substituting a state-specific protocol.
Interpret screening performance, false-positive risk, timing and handoff responsibilities.
topics: Dried blood spot system
State panel variation
False positives/negatives
Metabolic emergencies and escalation
Longitudinal follow-up
boardDomains: ABP: newborn care; emergency/acute illness; metabolic/genetic conditions
ABMGG: biochemical genetics, screening and prevention
units.casePractice: Fictional call from newborn-screening programme about an abnormal analyte; learner drafts a closed-loop handoff, not treatment orders.
units.assessment: Screen-positive response flowchart; rubric: distinguishes screen from diagnosis 30%, timely escalation 30%, safe communication 25%, acknowledges state variation 15%.

units.title: Pediatrics core: development, neurodevelopment, adolescence and acute care interfaces
prerequisites: Medical degree-level pediatrics; units 1–3.
objectives: Describe an age-appropriate developmental evaluation and when a genetic differential merits referral.
Integrate common pediatric, developmental-behavioral and mental-health contexts while avoiding diagnostic overshadowing.
Use age-specific acuity and escalation principles when suspected genetic disease coexists with acute illness.
topics: Milestones and global developmental delay
Behavioral and mental health context
Adolescent consent and family roles
Emergency red flags
Transitions and continuity
boardDomains: ABP: developmental-behavioral; adolescent medicine; mental health; emergency/acute illness
units.casePractice: Fictional adolescent with developmental history and new symptoms; separate urgent evaluation from etiologic workup.
units.assessment: Prioritization memo; rubric: identifies immediate risk 35%, developmental chronology 25%, appropriate referral/testing questions 25%, confidentiality/communication 15%.

units.title: Genetic testing strategy: karyotype, CMA, panels, exome and genome
prerequisites: Units 1–4; basic molecular biology.
objectives: Select a test strategy based on clinical question, variant class, limitations, availability and family preferences.
Explain why ES/GS is recommended first- or second-tier for defined pediatric CA/DD/ID populations in ACMG guidance and discuss local payer/lab differences.
Recognize important test blind spots, including repeat expansions, methylation disorders, balanced rearrangements, mosaicism and coverage gaps.
topics: Chromosomal microarray and karyotype
Targeted panels
ES/GS and trio design
Methylation/repeat testing
Reanalysis and diagnostic yield framing
Proportionate variant analysis and assay sensitivity/coverage (GenQA supplement)
Rare-disease variant assessment tools and clinical-laboratory workflow (GenQA supplement)
boardDomains: ABMGG: test selection, methods, limitations, lab interpretation
ABP: genetics and dysmorphology; developmental delay
units.casePractice: Fictional child with unexplained congenital anomalies and developmental delay; compare clinically plausible testing sequences.
units.assessment: One-page test-selection matrix; rubric: matches mechanism to method 35%, explains limits 30%, counseling/alternatives 20%, cites current source 15%.

units.title: Variant interpretation, segregation, databases and reclassification
prerequisites: Unit 5; basic molecular genetics.
objectives: Describe the ACMG/AMP five-class sequence variant framework and the evidence categories that contribute.
Distinguish a VUS from pathogenic/likely pathogenic evidence and avoid using a VUS alone for clinical decisions.
Use segregation, phenotype fit, population frequency, functional/technical limits and reanalysis appropriately.
topics: Population, computational, functional and segregation evidence
Phase and de novo status
ClinVar assertion review and conflict
Gene-disease validity
Reanalysis and uncertainty
Database provenance and interpretation workflows: ClinVar, ClinGen and population-frequency resources
Classification guidance and evidence limits in laboratory practice; never equate database concordance with an individual diagnosis
boardDomains: ABMGG: variant interpretation, laboratory methods, data resources
units.casePractice: Use public ClinVar assertions as a database-literacy exercise, not as a copied patient chart or independent clinical classification.
units.assessment: Structured variant memo; rubric: no overcalling 35%, evaluates evidence/quality 30%, phenotype & segregation 20%, transparent uncertainty 15%.

units.title: Genetic counseling, consent, family communication and ethical practice
prerequisites: Units 1–6.
objectives: Explain pre-/post-test counseling principles, including uncertain, secondary/incidental, familial and reproductive findings.
Discuss consent, assent, adolescent autonomy, confidentiality, stigma and culturally responsive shared decisions.
Communicate a nondiagnostic result and distinguish education from individualized counseling.
topics: Testing choices and consent
Secondary findings
Family communication and cascade testing
Privacy/insurance caveats with jurisdictional qualification
Return of results and nondiagnostic outcomes
Pretest/result communication and uncertainty as applied to variant databases; source webinar is laboratory-centred and requires pediatric counseling guidance
boardDomains: ABP: adolescent care; professionalism; family-centered care
units.casePractice: Fictional pretest discussion for trio sequencing; offer questions and teach-back, without collecting actual genetic or identifying data.
units.assessment: Recorded role-play transcript; rubric: balanced choices 30%, understands uncertainty 25%, age/family respect 25%, teach-back and documentation 20%.

units.title: Genotype–phenotype correlation across pediatric systems
prerequisites: Units 1–7.
objectives: Synthesize phenotype, inheritance and test results to generate a prioritized differential across neurologic, cardiac, ophthalmic, neuromuscular and multisystem presentations.
Recognize variable expression and phenocopies and avoid reasoning from one finding alone.
Identify when multidisciplinary input or specialty-directed surveillance is warranted.
topics: Neurodevelopment/epilepsy
Neuromuscular disease
Cardiovascular/connective-tissue disease
Ophthalmic disorders
Inflammatory/immune genetics
boardDomains: ABP: organ-system illness, development, cardiology/neurology contexts
ABMGG: clinical reasoning and syndrome recognition
units.casePractice: Compare fictional phenotype cards with ClinGen gene–disease curation status; do not treat associations as a patient diagnosis.
units.assessment: Differential table; rubric: breadth without unfocused list 25%, evidence weighting 30%, red flags 25%, source use 20%.

units.title: Therapeutics, pharmacogenomics, precision care and natural history
prerequisites: Units 1–8; pharmacology foundations.
objectives: Evaluate whether a molecular result is actionable and what additional clinical criteria are necessary.
Distinguish genotype-guided prescribing evidence from deterministic predictions; verify current labels/guidelines before use.
Describe follow-up, surveillance and therapy-specific risks at a conceptual level without prescribing or authorizing treatment.
topics: Pharmacogenomics and evidence levels
Disease-modifying therapeutics
Natural history and endpoints
Access/equity and evidence limitations
Ongoing re-evaluation
boardDomains: ABP: medication safety, chronic disease, family counseling
units.casePractice: Fictional decision memo comparing a test result with current authoritative label/guideline requirements; no drug/dose recommendation.
units.assessment: Evidence appraisal; rubric: source date/currentness 25%, actionability distinction 30%, risks and uncertainty 25%, equity/access 20%.

units.title: Prenatal, reproductive and pediatric cancer predisposition genetics
prerequisites: Units 1–9.
objectives: Distinguish screening from diagnostic prenatal testing and describe referral/counseling pathways.
Recognize family-history and phenotype clues warranting cancer predisposition assessment without overclaiming risk.
Describe how pediatric and adult-onset findings affect family communication and age-appropriate care.
topics: Prenatal and maternal-child genetics
Carrier screening/NIPS limits
Cancer predisposition and family history
Tumor surveillance principles
Genomic findings with adult-onset implications
units.casePractice: Fictional family-history pedigree: identify missing history, referral threshold questions and family communication needs.
units.assessment: Pedigree-to-plan exercise; rubric: separates screening/diagnosis 25%, family-history interpretation 30%, counseling/referral 25%, source/date checking 20%.

units.title: Biochemical genetics, metabolism and acute–chronic integration
prerequisites: Units 1–10; biochemistry and pediatric acute-care foundations.
objectives: Relate pathway-level reasoning to possible inborn-error presentations and urgent specialist assessment.
Interpret screening and laboratory data as clues rather than definitive diagnoses.
Explain how biochemical, genomic and clinical evidence can be integrated and when specialist laboratory interpretation is required.
topics: Metabolic pathways and inheritance
Acute decompensation differential
Clinical biochemical laboratory workflow
Therapeutic monitoring concepts
Coordination with metabolic teams
boardDomains: ABP: newborn care, emergency, inpatient pediatrics
units.casePractice: Fictional metabolite pattern exercise using invented values; explicitly not a real patient and not an actionable treatment plan.
units.assessment: Mechanism map; rubric: plausible pathway reasoning 30%, test caveats 25%, escalation 25%, no fabricated certainty 20%.

units.title: Integrated longitudinal case conference, documentation and board-style synthesis
prerequisites: Units 1–11.
objectives: Integrate an age-appropriate history, examination, phenotype, differential, testing choice, counseling and follow-up plan.
Explain how ABP and ABMGG are distinct boards with separate exam/certification requirements.
Reflect on uncertainty and the boundary between self-study and clinical competence.
topics: Case synthesis
Communication and documentation
Continuity and handoffs
Quality/equity considerations
Board blueprint review and deliberate practice
boardDomains: ABMGG: integrated clinical genetics competencies and professional practice
ABP: general pediatrics content outline; cross-domain integration
units.casePractice: Capstone is a clearly fictional composite vignette; learners must not submit identifiable patient information.
units.assessment: Capstone rubric: immediate safety/triage 20%, phenotype and differential 20%, test/result interpretation 25%, counseling/follow-up 20%, transparent limits and citations 15%.

assignment.name: Pedigree and phenotype synthesis
assignment.deliverable: Deidentified-free fictional pedigree, structured phenotype inventory and ranked differential.

assignment.name: Test selection and variant-report conference
assignment.deliverable: Compare two clinically plausible test pathways for a fictional pediatric CA/DD/ID vignette; interpret one public database record without copying images or patient-level data.

assignment.name: Newborn-screen response and closed-loop handoff
assignment.deliverable: Educational flow diagram using a fictional abnormal-screen callback; local protocols must be consulted in real practice.

assignment.name: Capstone board-style case conference
assignment.deliverable: Fictional longitudinal pediatric case: problem representation, focused differential, test interpretation, family communication and follow-up questions.

formative: Retrieval questions and spaced review after each unit
summative: 10 original questions in this package; each has a keyed explanation but is not validated exam content
assessment.masteryRule: A local course suggestion only: revise work below 80% rubric attainment and discuss missed concepts with an appropriately qualified clinician. This is not a board-passing threshold or predictor.
assessment.rubricOverview: Assess source use, reasoning, safety framing, uncertainty, communication and age-specific context—not memorization alone. No diagnosis, treatment, procedure or independent patient care is authorized.

studyHours.basis: Transparent suggested study schedule only: 36 hours of target recorded lecture time, approximately 18 hours of readings/notes, and 6 hours of question/assignment work. Only the actually verified public recording hours below count as existing video. No study-hour estimate is added to video totals; planned original clips do not count.

mapping.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine
mapping.name: Combined Pediatrics and Medical Genetics Residency
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: The supplied public directory URL names this exact combined clinical physician residency and describes eligible graduates for separate ABP and ABMGG examinations. Johns Hopkins Department of Genetic Medicine gives fuller current public curriculum detail: four-year integrated programme (approval in 2014), first year pediatrics, alternating six-month pediatrics/genetics periods in years 2–4, final six months individualized, training at Johns Hopkins Hospital and affiliated sites, additional research fellowship encouraged but not part of four-year minimum. The 2026–27 JHU catalogue calls it a four-year curriculum meeting ABP and ABMGG requirements and describes the residency programmes as ACGME-accredited. The public programme page does not expose a resident-specific current block schedule. Current ACGME minimum combined requirements are cited separately; no claim was made that each Hopkins local rotation was independently verified in the ACGME ADS finder.

unitMap.text: Foundations: human variation, inheritance and clinical genetics
Clinical genetics encounter, dysmorphology and phenotype encoding
Newborn screening, biochemical genetics and time-critical follow-up
Pediatrics core: development, neurodevelopment, adolescence and acute care interfaces
Genetic testing strategy: karyotype, CMA, panels, exome and genome
coveredTopics: Proportionate variant analysis and assay sensitivity/coverage (GenQA supplement)
Rare-disease variant assessment tools and clinical-laboratory workflow (GenQA supplement)

unitMap.text: Variant interpretation, segregation, databases and reclassification
coveredTopics: Population, computational, functional and segregation evidence
Database provenance and interpretation workflows: ClinVar, ClinGen and population-frequency resources
Classification guidance and evidence limits in laboratory practice; never equate database concordance with an individual diagnosis

unitMap.text: Genetic counseling, consent, family communication and ethical practice
coveredTopics: Return of results and nondiagnostic outcomes
Pretest/result communication and uncertainty as applied to variant databases; source webinar is laboratory-centred and requires pediatric counseling guidance

unitMap.text: Genotype–phenotype correlation across pediatric systems
Therapeutics, pharmacogenomics, precision care and natural history
Prenatal, reproductive and pediatric cancer predisposition genetics
Biochemical genetics, metabolism and acute–chronic integration
Integrated longitudinal case conference, documentation and board-style synthesis
coveredTopics: Board blueprint review and deliberate practice

topicGaps: General pediatric breadth remains the largest video gap: no comparable current recorded coverage was verified for ordinary ambulatory pediatrics, newborn/infant care, ED/inpatient/PICU/NICU and developmental-behavioral/adolescent medicine.
Hands-on physical examination, dysmorphology assessment, procedural skill, supervised case exposure and clinical judgment cannot be acquired or assessed through these recordings or scripts.

Time-critical metabolic decompensation, biochemical test interpretation, disorder-specific confirmation and state newborn-screen follow-up still need source-checked, local-protocol-specific supervised instruction; the packet’s original CDC content distinguishes population screening from diagnosis.

The added GenQA recordings improve exposure to variant-analysis tools, assay sensitivity/CNV interpretation and databases, but are laboratory-centred and do not replace clinical genetics supervision or current patient-specific laboratory interpretation.

Phenotype-first pediatric evaluation, assay selection across CMA/ES/GS/repeat/methylation mechanisms, VUS communication, consent/secondary findings, and developmental assessment remain insufficiently covered by the public recordings and are addressed in authored scripts only as education.

Most pre-existing NHGRI recordings are approximately 12–14 years old. Therapeutic indications, screening panels, eligibility, board rules and any time-sensitive claims must be rechecked against current authoritative sources before use.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician residency — an integrated combined residency in general pediatrics and Clinical Genetics and Genomics; not a research-only appointment, lab fellowship, genetic-counseling programme or generic directory label.

American Board of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ABMGG), Clinical Genetics and Genomics
medical.boardStatus: Separate component board certifications and examinations exist. Johns Hopkins states successful completion of this four-year combined programme qualifies trainees to pursue the ABP and ABMGG certification examinations; ABP requires all four years completed before its certifying exam. No course enrollee is thereby eligible. ABMGG board eligibility and all current board requirements must be verified with the boards.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Self-study is not accredited training and grants no eligibility. The Hopkins programme page describes board-exam eligibility after successful completion; ABMGG pathway rules and ABP rules apply independently. No guarantee of eligibility, admission or passing. Checked 2026-10-07.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine
officialProgrammes.name: Combined Pediatrics and Medical Genetics Residency
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: The supplied public directory URL names this exact combined clinical physician residency and describes eligible graduates for separate ABP and ABMGG examinations. Johns Hopkins Department of Genetic Medicine gives fuller current public curriculum detail: four-year integrated programme (approval in 2014), first year pediatrics, alternating six-month pediatrics/genetics periods in years 2–4, final six months individualized, training at Johns Hopkins Hospital and affiliated sites, additional research fellowship encouraged but not part of four-year minimum. The 2026–27 JHU catalogue calls it a four-year curriculum meeting ABP and ABMGG requirements and describes the residency programmes as ACGME-accredited. The public programme page does not expose a resident-specific current block schedule. Current ACGME minimum combined requirements are cited separately; no claim was made that each Hopkins local rotation was independently verified in the ACGME ADS finder.

programmeSourceScope.exactProgramClassification: A clinical physician combined residency—not a medical-school course, categorical-only genetics residency, research-only postdoctoral supplement, laboratory fellowship, directory category, or non-physician track. Medical Genetics and Genomics is an ABMGG physician primary specialty; the combined pathway has separate ABP and ABMGG certification exams.

institutionalVariants.officialName: Combined Pediatrics and Medical Genetics Residency

programmeSourceScope.accreditationQualifier: JHU catalogue describes the residency offerings as ACGME-accredited; ACGME publishes current combined Pediatrics/Medical Genetics minimum requirements. No successful live lookup of the active programme’s current ADS record/block diagram was made; do not infer unobserved accreditation details from the generic directory label.
programmeSourceScope.whatIsNotIncluded: Research postdoctoral positions, categorical genetics-only residency, medical biochemical genetics fellowship, LGG/CBG laboratory fellowships, genetic counselling and generic directory categories are not counted as this physician specialty or as board eligibility.

sourceCaveats: The public Hopkins page has a historical note that the programme used to be five years; the newer programme and 2026–27 catalogue identify the current integrated curriculum as four years.
